headline: CONSULTANCY SCAMS
description: CONSULTANCY SCAMS: The recent suicide committed by a young girl in Islamabad has highlighted the vulnerability of...
author: From the Newspaper
article_text:
CONSULTANCY SCAMS: The recent suicide committed by a young girl in Islamabad has highlighted the vulnerability of Pakistani students at the hands of fraudulent education consultancies. Many families sell property and borrow money to fulfil their children’s dreams of studying abroad. Unfortunately, unscrupulous agents exploit their aspirations through false promises, fabricated documents and misleading scholarship claims. Pakistan urgently needs stronger regulation of education consultancies. The authorities concerned should establish transparent registration mechanisms, provide accessible complaint and verification systems, and take strict action against offenders. Universities should also facilitate direct verification of admission letters and scholarship offers.

Dr Farooq Ahmad Islamabad

ANARKALI FOOD STREET: The poor hygiene conditions at Lahore’s famous Anarkali food street require immediate attention of the authorities concerned. There are open drains at several points, causing foul smell and becoming a breeding ground for mosquitoes during the rainy season. Food at the stalls is often left uncovered, while some food handlers prepare and serve it without gloves, proper head covering and without following basic hygiene measures. The relevant authorities need to carry out regular inspections, cover the open drains and ensure that food is properly covered.

Muhammad Hanzla Lahore

FREQUENT POWER CUTS: For some people, a power cut means waiting a few minutes till the power supply gets restored. For others, it means losing a day’s earnings or spending another sleepless night. Frequent electricity outages are more than an inconvenience; they are a problem that affects people’s ability to work, study and carry on with their daily lives. What makes the situation more frustrating is the uncertainty. K-Electric (KE) should provide timely updates about scheduled loadshedding so that area residents may plan their everyday tasks accordingly.

Yamna Uzair Karachi

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: Sheer exploitation
description: THE Behbood Savings Certificates were officially launched by the government in July 2003 as a social welfare...
author: From the Newspaper
article_text:
THE Behbood Savings Certificates were officially launched by the government in July 2003 as a social welfare initiative to provide a secure and stable monthly income to the elderly and the disabled. Initially, the scheme was exempt from tax and Zakat deductions, and one could nominate an individual to inherit the funds once the investor ceased to exist. Over the last more than 20 years, there have been a number of changes that have all gone against the investors, adding more layers of vulnerability to the already vulnerable.

Senior citizens, instead of being looked after when they need it most, have been left high and dry to fight loneliness and the high cost of living. The marginalised citizens are mostly white-collared professionals who gave the best part of their lives to society and paid all due taxes. They have now been hit by a triple-edged sword.

The profit rates have drastically been reduced, a five per cent tax has been imposed, and the option of nominee has been taken away, leaving the inheritors to keep filling the coffers of solicitors and the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra).

Yet another trick has been played on them in the shape of changes related to joint accounts with an ‘either or survivor’ clause. The least the government could do is to consider withdrawing the 5pc tax as its impact will not be too astronomical compared to the concessions that are being extended to traders and exporters.

Khaled Islamabad

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: Failed governance
description: THIS refers to the report ‘Residents write to CM Murad, urge halt to reconstruction on Nehr-i-Khayyam’ (Oct 23)....
author: From the Newspaper
article_text:
THIS refers to the report ‘Residents write to CM Murad, urge halt to reconstruction on Nehr-i-Khayyam’ (Oct 23). The project is truly a classic case study of institutional failure in Karachi.

In his previous stint, the chief minister had announced the rehabilitation of Nehr-i-Khayyam, one of the city’s most prominent storm water drains cutting across the Clifton Boat Basin area. A local non-governmental organisation (NGO) was taken on board in 2019, and the project was expected to be completed in a year. The proposal was to establish a separate line for sewage, which is being dumped into the drain, and then create a public space around it. The project failed.

Subsequently, through the Competitive and Liveable City of Karachi (CLICK) project, a neighbourhood improvement scheme was launched for the Clifton Block 5 area. The World Bank-funded project helped to make new parks, and it also rehabili- tated the area around Nehr-i-Khayyam.

Millions of rupees were invested to construct a pedestrian walkway right beside the drain. A few months later, the current city mayor launched a project related to the dumping of sewage in the drain. Hence, the entire newly-built pedestrian track around the area was destroyed, and Nehr-i-Khayyam again became a construction site. The project was to be completed by June 2026. That did not happen.

Meanwhile, the provincial government claims to be working in Karachi, and continues opposing an empowered local government system or making Karachi an administrative unit, seeming satisfied with the inadequate resources provided to its own mayor. Boasting about his performance by doing the bare minimum — visiting the city while it is being flooded, improving basic facilities like reconstruc- ting some roads, putting paver blocks in some streets, and improving lighting — the mayor often acts ‘surprised’ by the criticism he attracts.

All this while, pollutants and solid waste continue to be thrown around and put to fire on the outskirts of Nehr-i-Khayyam, leaving toxic fumes wafting around resi-dential areas.

All the money invested to improve the situation has been wasted. These cosmetic activities in an institutionally fractured city are unable to hide deep-seated institutional governance issues, where the provincial government, the local government and the city administration have together failed to execute a simple project that merely involves improving a storm-water drain within a city area.

Mahiba Jaffari Karachi

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

Meanwhile, the provincial government claims to be working in Karachi, and continues opposing an empowered local government system or making Karachi an administrative unit, seeming satisfied with the inadequate resources provided to its own mayor. Boasting about his performance by doing the bare minimum — visiting the city while it is being flooded, improving basic facilities like reconstruc- ting some roads, putting paver blocks in some streets, and improving lighting — the mayor often acts ‘surprised’ by the criticism he attracts.
All this while, pollutants and solid waste continue to be thrown around and put to fire on the outskirts of Nehr-i-Khayyam, leaving toxic fumes wafting around resi-dential areas.

All the money invested to improve the situation has been wasted. These cosmetic activities in an institutionally fractured city are unable to hide deep-seated institutional governance issues, where the provincial government, the local government and the city administration have together failed to execute a simple project that merely involves improving a storm-water drain within a city area.

headline: A cultural icon forgotten already?
description: MY father, film star Syed Kamal, would always say: “We are dead only when we are forgotten”. There are artists...
author: From the Newspaper
article_text:
MY father, film star Syed Kamal, would always say: “We are dead only when we are forgotten”. There are artists who entertain a nation, and then there are artists who help build its cultural identity. Kamal belonged to the latter. One of the country’s most recognisable film and television personalities, he appeared in more than 300 movies, worked extensively in television, produced and directed films, hosted TV programmes, mentored young performers and established institutions intended to give future generations of artists a platform.

Yet today, his name is largely absent from the national conversation about the pioneers of Pakistani entertainment. That is an omission worth correcting.

Kamal became a popular and award-winning movie icon during the golden era of Pakistani cinema in the 1960s and 1970s. As a producer and director, he used cinema to comment on society. His 1973 classic, Insaan Aur Gadha, was not conventional entertainment; it was a sharp political satire that explored the absurdities of power and the struggles of the ordinary citizens. He produced and directed more than a dozen films, and his eagerness to speak to society rather than simply perform an act was characteristic of the man that he was. His television programmes, including The Kamal Show and Har Taan Hai Deepak, made him a household name in an era when television itself was becoming an important part of Pakistan’s cultural landscape.

But perhaps the most important part of his legacy is what he did for others, establishing the Pakistan Film and TV Academy and the Karachi Film Guild, creating platforms for training, development and professional growth within the industry. He also created opportunities to discover new performers through talent-spotting programmes, including his Take 2 Acting Challenge.

Later in life, Kamal also participated in electoral politics and engaged with issues beyond the entertainment industry. He died in Karachi on Oct 1, 2009. His contribution remains worthy of national recognition. As such, should Kamal be remembered only through his films and television recordings, or should the government formally recognise the contribution he made to cultural heritage?

Mariam KamalKarachi

headline: Vicious demons of political narratives
description: SOME political parties possess a peculiar advantage: they gain political fame not necessarily through their own...
author: From the Newspaper
article_text:
SOME political parties possess a peculiar advantage: they gain political fame not necessarily through their own achievements, but through populism and the mistakes of their opponents. The political journey of the main opposition leader, currently in prison for financial corruption, raises an important question about whether political popularity in Pakistan is earned through governance, or created through the failures of rival parties.

When the man was removed from office through a parliamentary vote of no confidence in 2022, he transformed his removal into a powerful political narrative. Rather than marking the end of its political influence, the event became a rallying

point for its supporters. The mistakes and controversies of its opponents helped keep the party at the centre of national politics even as questions about the merit of its own governance remained relevant.

A similar concern is related to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), where terrorism, educational shortcomings, gender dis-parities and economic difficulties demand urgent attention. However, controversies surrounding governor’s rule and the provincial political leadership have potentially shifted public attention from these persistent problems towards grave confrontation, even victimisation.

Whenever the government and its allies take action, the party portrays it as an attack on its political mandate, and, in the process, uses the action as yet another opportunity to mobilise its supporters.

This surely does not mean that the party has achieved nothing of substance. Indeed, it does not mean either that other political parties have achieved anything of subs-tance. Rather, it highlights a troubling feature of Pakistan’s political culture: a party can gain public sympathy on the basis of its opponents’ mistakes without necessarily demonstrating corresponding success in governance.

Ultimately, the actual measure of any political party should be its ability to improve people’s lives, not its capacity to turn every political setback into a victory of public perception.

When opponents repeatedly strengthen a party through their own miscalculations, political fame becomes easier to acquire than political performance, and ordinary citizens continue waiting for solutions.

headline: Exchange hack
description: ON Thursday, the largest cryptocurrency heist in history saw some $6.3bn drained from exchange platform Binance’s...
author: Editorial
article_text:
ON Thursday, the largest cryptocurrency heist in history saw some $6.3bn drained from exchange platform Binance’s own wallets. Most of the funds were moved out in about 20 minutes. The hack dwarfed the previous record, of some $1.5bn from rival exchange Bybit in February 2025. Binance’s own investigation initially suggested that the laptop of one of its engineers had been compromised, which allowed attackers to gain access to an internal service used to submit withdrawals. It later emerged that this had been a sophisticated attack involving multiple breach points in Binance’s systems, malicious software that covered its tracks as it operated, and abuse of a feature of the Ethereum network to bypass the exchange’s normal approval controls. Blockchain analytics firms have attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking group. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, has suspended withdrawals as it reviews security.

Though Binance has said it will cover all user losses, news of this incident has shaken the crypto sphere. It also raises serious questions — about custody standards, licensing conditions for exchanges, and who bears the losses when things go wrong — for countries in the process of embracing cryptocurrency, including Pakistan. The fact is that Binance is considerably more experienced in the crypto trade than most new entrants and regulators. If its security and operational controls can be compromised, then potentially anyone can be at risk. Until early last year, Pakistan treated crypto as a regulatory no-go area. The authorities have since reversed gear. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao has served as a strategic adviser to the Pakistan Crypto Council since April 2025, and in December 2025 the finance ministry signed an MoU with Binance to explore tokenising up to $2bn in sovereign assets. The exchange’s troubles are therefore of direct concern to Islamabad. But though embracing technology is understandable and perhaps also commendable, policymakers must ensure that the risks that come with dealing in crypto are also being actively assessed and addressed. This incident is a timely reminder that the cost of a security failure can be immense. The authorities need to understand what they are getting into, and make provisions to mitigate risk.

ON Thursday, the largest cryptocurrency heist in history saw some $6.3bn drained from exchange platform Binance’s own wallets. Most of the funds were moved out in about 20 minutes. The hack dwarfed the previous record, of some $1.5bn from rival exchange Bybit in February 2025. Binance’s own investigation initially suggested that the laptop of one of its engineers had been compromised, which allowed attackers to gain access to an internal service used to submit withdrawals. It later emerged that this had been a sophisticated attack involving multiple breach points in Binance’s systems, malicious software that covered its tracks as it operated, and abuse of a feature of the Ethereum network to bypass the exchange’s normal approval controls. Blockchain analytics firms have attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking group. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, has suspended withdrawals as it reviews security.

It also raises serious questions — about custody standards, licensing conditions for exchanges, and who bears the losses when things go wrong — for countries in the process of embracing cryptocurrency, including Pakistan. The fact is that Binance is considerably more experienced in the crypto trade than most new entrants and regulators. If its security and operational controls can be compromised, then potentially anyone can be at risk. Until early last year, Pakistan treated crypto as a regulatory no-go area. headline: From The Past Pages Of Dawn: 1951: Seventy-five years ago: Phoney post office
description: KARACHI: A phoney post office and a postal money orders racket were unearthed by the Pakistan Special Police on...
author: From the Newspaper
article_text:
KARACHI: A phoney post office and a postal money orders racket were unearthed by the Pakistan Special Police on Wednesday [Oct 31] when they hauled up three members of an alleged gang.

The Police, who had been informed of the racket involving several thousand rupees, managed to locate one of the addressees of the bogus money orders.

The money order form gave out that Rs 300 were sent by a person from a certain town in East Pakistan to a man in Karachi. The money was to be paid through the Lalukhet Post Office.

A trap was laid and the addressee was apprehended while receiving the money. Investigation led to two more arrests and also the discovery of a phoney post office in Gizri Hills, a city outskirt.

The phoney post office was equipped with all paraphernalia of making entries, stamps and forged signatures on the forged money order forms which were obtained from [the] local post offices.

The forged money orders were mixed with the incoming dak and the money was paid to the addressees from the local post offices.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: From The Past Pages Of Dawn: 1976: Fifty Years Ago: Driving by ‘minors’
description: CASES of driving of vehicles by under-age boys and girls in the City [Karachi] have increased alarmingly and are a...
author: A Correspondent
article_text:
CASES of driving of vehicles by under-age boys and girls in the City [Karachi] have increased alarmingly and are a danger to human lives on roads, this was revealed by a spokesman of the Police Department. …

He appealed to car and scooter owners not to allow their sons and daughters, who are still ‘minors’ under law, to drive their vehicles, causing traffic accidents in the City.

He said such dangerous practices by members of affluent families have already claimed a number of lives (due to rash and negligent driving).

He also advised drivers not to ply their vehicles with ‘glaring head lights’ which may cause accidents. He said they should dip their lights. …

[Meanwhile, as per a report by Our Staff Reporter,] a supersonic jet fighter plane of the PAF broke the sound barrier over Karachi skies at about 4.55 p.m. yesterday [Oct 31].

The big boom, heard all over the City, alerted the Fire Brigade and Police and some citizens complained of broken window panes.

Official sources later confirmed the breaking of the sound barrier by the supersonic while on a low flight.

Citizens confirmed they had seen two supersonic jet fighter planes in the skies.

headline: OVERHEARD
description: Have you seen Kylie Jenner walking the ramp in Victoria’s Secret’s [$50] million [Fantasy] bra? People are appreciating it without
author: From InpaperMagazine
article_text:
“Paid propaganda against a film is upsetting because the industry ends up paying the price. Reviews appear the morning after a Friday release, sometimes by people who haven’t even watched the film, using similar words.”

— Faysal Quraishi, actor

“A bad director will remain a bad director, no matter how many good actors they assemble in their movies. Period.”

— Shamoon Abbasi, actor and director

“Have you seen Kylie Jenner walking the ramp in Victoria’s Secret’s [$50] million [Fantasy] bra? People are appreciating it without thinking about the fact that Victoria’s Secret was secretly involved in the Epstein files. They’re also completely discarding the fact that a [$50] million bra could literally give so many homeless people a home. Where are women’s rights and gender equality?”

— Naeema Butt, actor

“People say individuals like Abu Bakar and his mother [in Dar-i-Nijaat] don’t exist in real life. Why are basic human traits like kindness, empathy, forgiveness and overlooking others’ flaws becoming so rare in our society that characters who display them seem unreal to us?”

— Umera Ahmed, writer

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

Iran’s national security chief Mohsen Rezaei says Tehran has repeatedly stated that the seven conditions announced by it must be fulfilled.

“If the conditions are met, the path of diplomacy will be open,” he said in an X post, adding that, however, “if any action is taken against the country, in accordance with the supreme leader’s […], we will deliver devastating blows to the aggressor using new weaponry”.

headline: Trump says US still has to 'take care' of one or two targets in Iran
description: President Donald Trump says that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but it still has to “take...
article_text:
President Donald Trump says that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but it still has to “take care of” one or two targets including a suspected nuclear site known as Pickaxe Mountain, AFP reports.

Trump maintains that negotiations with Iran are “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable.” The US president reiterates that the US is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it has decimated Iran’s military and nuclear program.

“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump has told reporters at his Florida residence.

“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he adds, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.

The Iranian government has denied any nuclear work is carried out there.

headline: LPG price twice the official rate in open market
description: Ogra notifies about Rs15 per kg increase in gas price; LPG selling for up to Rs630 per kg in open market while company-operated franchises are charging up to Rs400 per kg.
author: Kalbe Ali
article_text:
• Ogra notifies about Rs15 per kg increase in gas price• Association warns of strike from Nov 16 over new LPG policy

ISLAMABAD: As the government again notified an increase in the price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for November, its price in the open market is twice as high as the official rate amid a shortage of LPG due to the US-Iran war.

In a notification on Saturday, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) notified Rs294,075 per tonne for November compared to Rs279,341 in the previous month. Following the increase, the official retail rate of an 11.8 kg domestic cylinder of LPG is Rs3,470, up by Rs173. The official LPG rate is Rs294 per kilogramme.

The oil and gas regulator said that the LPG producer price was linked with Saudi Aramco-CP and the US dollar exchange rate. It added that compared to the previous month, Saudi Aramco-CP had increased by 6.47 per cent, while the average dollar exchange rate had slightly decreased by 0.12pc, resulting in an increase in the LPG consumer price by Rs14.73 per kg.

In the open market, LPG is selling for up to Rs630 per kg, while the company-operated franchises are charging up to Rs400 per kg, with many warning that the crisis would compound due to the gas shortage.

LPG Distributors Association of Pakistan Chairman Irfan Khokhar said that the situation was serious because of the Iran border closure. He said at least 70 per cent of LPG was imported from Iran, while only 30pc was locally produced. “The government has to make serious efforts to control market manipulations,” Mr Khokhar added.

On the other hand, LPG marketing companies thre­atened to shut down their businesses from Nov 16 if the private sector was sidelined in the upcoming LPG policy. Pakistan LPG Marketers Association Cha­irman Ali Haider warned that they will observe a strike from Nov 16 if the government implemented the policy. He said the government should not reverse the deregulation of LPG, adding that the gas was in short supply due to the Iran border closure.

“Out of around 1.3 million tonnes, only around 225,000 is imported from the Gulf, and that too has been mainly imported by the private sector,” he said, adding that the ProGas terminal at Port Qasim was under the control of the Sui Southern Gas Company which “imported LPG around seven months back”. The association also wrote a letter to Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, stating the draft policy sent to the prime minister had no input from the private sector. The association called for the complete deregulation of the LPG sector.

It said the 2016 LPG policy imposed Rs4,669 per tonne petroleum development levy on locally produced LPG. This was imposed to provide subsidies to the state-owned entities such as the PSO, Parco, and SSGC to import LPG during winters and in any emergency, like the current scenario. “Despite billions of rupees collected in terms of PDL through this formula, the state-owned entities have failed to import LPG during these days,” Mr Haider alleged.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

In a notification on Saturday, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) notified Rs294,075 per tonne for November compared to Rs279,341 in the previous month. Following the increase, the official retail rate of an 11.8 kg domestic cylinder of LPG is Rs3,470, up by Rs173. The official LPG rate is Rs294 per kilogramme.

He said at least 70 per cent of LPG was imported from Iran, while only 30pc was locally produced. “The government has to make serious efforts to control market manipulations,” Mr Khokhar added.

Pakistan LPG Marketers Association Cha­irman Ali Haider warned that they will observe a strike from Nov 16 if the government implemented the policy. headline: Erdogan slams Black Sea shipping attacks
description: Says attacks on civilian vessels ‘unacceptable’; Zelensky discusses security, peace efforts with Turkish president.
author: AFP
article_text:
ISTANBUL / WASHINGTON: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Saturday that attacks targeting civilian vessels in the Black Sea were unacceptable, urging Russia and Ukraine to “act responsibly”.

Despite its ties with both Russia and Ukraine, Turkiye has been angered by attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.

“It is clear that attacks against civilian vessels and actions that further escalate tensions in the Black Sea serve no one’s interests,” Erdogan told a news conference with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in Istanbul.

“We cannot accept these attacks under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what justification is offered. We call on all parties to act responsibly on this matter,” he said.

Says attacks on civilian vessels ‘unacceptable’; Zelensky discusses security, peace efforts with Turkish president

Ankara has sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine to end strikes on civilian ships, but says the two countries have failed to act on it.

Zelensky accused Russia of making the situation in the Black Sea difficult, saying a significant part of his talks with Erdogan had focused on security concerns in the region.

Erdogan said discussions aimed at restoring the safety of navigation in the Black Sea would continue.

“I believe that reaching an agreement on this issue would also give fresh impetus to efforts to secure lasting peace in Ukraine,” he added.

Erdogan also welcomed renewed momentum behind efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war through “diplomatic means”, referring in particular to US President Donald Trump’s initiative.

“At this point, we maintain that there can be no losers in a just peace,” he said.

Last week, the Kremlin said the next round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US was expected to resume in November in the UAE.

Zelensky said he had discussed the format of the talks with Erdogan, as well as other possibilities, “in particular the possibilities of involving Turkiye, involving Europe, involving all partners”.

Patriot missiles

The Trump administration has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, the US State Department said, but the Ukrainian president warned that deliveries could take years.

The approval, which will be submitted to Congress for review, comes after weeks of complaints by Ukrainian authorities that their supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling.

“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defence capabilities,” the department said in a statement.

The statement did not provide an estimate of when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.

However, Zelensky said late on Friday in a post on X that “deliveries may begin only in a few years”.

headline: US to deport 150 Afghan immigrants back to Kabul
description: NYT reports that first flight could leave as soon as Monday.
author: AFP
article_text:
WASHINGTON: President Don­­ald Trump’s administration plans to deport more than 150 Afghan immigrants back to Afghanistan via Pakistan, US media reported, a move advocacy groups say could endanger their lives.

Trump last year issued travel bans for a number of countries, including Afghanistan, as part of a broad immigration crackdown, and sought to end deportation protections for Afghans, some of whom were granted special immigrant visas following the August 2021 takeover by the Taliban.

More than 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported in the latest push, The New York Times reported on Friday, citing three unnamed US officials, and the first flight could leave as soon as Monday.

Among those expected to be deported are relatives of Afghans who assisted the US military in the country prior to the fall of Kabul, according to AfghanEvac, a group seeking to help former Afghan allies.

While the US cannot arrange deportations directly to Afgha­n­istan, the officials told the Times that Pakistan will oversee their expulsion to Afghanistan.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: Cost of provinces
description: Political parties demanding new provinces must explain how they intend to pay for them and what improvements citizens can expect.
author: Editorial
article_text:
THE cost would be steep. We all knew that. An Islamabad-based think tank has now put figures to those costs. That gives a fiscal dimension to a debate that has largely been driven by political demands and promises of better administration.

The Policy Research Institute of Market Economy estimates that creating two more provinces in Punjab could add Rs47bn to Rs57bn to annual recurring expenditure. The bill could rise to Rs610bn-Rs730bn if all the country’s 30 divisional units were turned into provinces.

Every new province would require a permanent administrative and political structure, including a governor, chief minister, assembly, secretariat and high court. Their salaries, operating expenses and overheads would have to be met year after year, leaving less money for development.

The figures expose a major weakness in the argument for creating more provinces: political and administrative restructuring is often presented as an inexpensive way to make government more responsive. It is not.

Smaller administrative units create another layer of government whose costs would be hard to justify. If a substantial portion of their allocations goes towards maintaining political and administrative establishments, little would remain for schools, hospitals and other essential services. Citizens promised better governance could end up paying for an expensive new tier without seeing much improvement.

There is, of course, a real case for reorganising provincial boundaries.

Punjab’s size and population, regional disparities and the sense of political and economic neglect in its southern districts cannot be dismissed. The demand for a separate South Punjab province reflects genuine grievances over unequal development. But these grievances cannot be resolved simply by creating new capitals, assemblies and secretariats. Nor should the fiscal argument be used to brush aside legitimate demands for political representation and administrative autonomy.

Can the same objectives be achieved through empowered local governments?

Political parties’ record of repeatedly suspending, delaying or weakening elected LGs suggests that the problem is less the size of provinces than the reluctance of political leadership to devolve power and resources.

Functional LGs, with predictable funding, elected representatives and clearly defined responsibilities, could take decision-making nearer to citizens without multiplying provincial overheads.

Any proposal for provincial restructuring must show how it would improve public services. It must also establish how new units would finance recurring expenditure. The creation of provinces is a long-term fiscal and constitutional commitment. Political parties demanding new provinces must explain how they intend to pay for them and what improvements citizens can expect.

article_html:
THE cost would be steep. We all knew that. An Islamabad-based think tank has now put figures to those costs. That gives a fiscal dimension to a debate that has largely been driven by political demands and promises of better administration.

The Policy Research Institute of Market Economy estimates that creating two more provinces in Punjab could add Rs47bn to Rs57bn to annual recurring expenditure. The bill could rise to Rs610bn-Rs730bn if all the country’s 30 divisional units were turned into provinces.

Every new province would require a permanent administrative and political structure, including a governor, chief minister, assembly, secretariat and high court. Their salaries, operating expenses and overheads would have to be met year after year, leaving less money for development.

The figures expose a major weakness in the argument for creating more provinces: political and administrative restructuring is often presented as an inexpensive way to make government more responsive. It is not.

Smaller administrative units create another layer of government whose costs would be hard to justify. If a substantial portion of their allocations goes towards maintaining political and administrative establishments, little would remain for schools, hospitals and other essential services. Citizens promised better governance could end up paying for an expensive new tier without seeing much improvement.

There is, of course, a real case for reorganising provincial boundaries.

Punjab’s size and population, regional disparities and the sense of political and economic neglect in its southern districts cannot be dismissed. The demand for a separate South Punjab province reflects genuine grievances over unequal development. But these grievances cannot be resolved simply by creating new capitals, assemblies and secretariats. Nor should the fiscal argument be used to brush aside legitimate demands for political representation and administrative autonomy.

Can the same objectives be achieved through empowered local governments?

Political parties’ record of repeatedly suspending, delaying or weakening elected LGs suggests that the problem is less the size of provinces than the reluctance of political leadership to devolve power and resources.

Functional LGs, with predictable funding, elected representatives and clearly defined responsibilities, could take decision-making nearer to citizens without multiplying provincial overheads.

Any proposal for provincial restructuring must show how it would improve public services. It must also establish how new units would finance recurring expenditure. The creation of provinces is a long-term fiscal and constitutional commitment. Political parties demanding new provinces must explain how they intend to pay for them and what improvements citizens can expect.

headline: Islamabad High Court bars FIR mention in character certificates after acquittal
description: Rules such mention violates constitutional rights, including dignity and freedom of movement.
author: Malik Asad
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has ruled that police cannot mention an FIR in the character certificate of a citizen who has been acquitted in the case, declaring any such certificate unlawful and invalid.

Justice Ayyaz Shaukat, while deciding a public interest petition, directed the Inspector General of Police, Islamabad, to establish a formal mechanism to ensure that references to criminal cases ending in acquittal are not included in character certificates issued to citizens.

The court observed that citizens should not be compelled to approach courts to exercise rights already guaranteed under the law.

It held that following an acquittal, there was no legal justification for portraying an individual as an accused or criminal through a police-issued character certificate.

Rules such mention violates constitutional rights, including dignity and freedom of movement

Allowing the petition, the court ordered the removal of a reference to an FIR registered at Shalimar Police Station from the petitioner’s character certificate.

The judgement clarified that although police could maintain internal records of criminal cases for official purposes, such information could not be disclosed in character certificates issued to citizens, particularly when these were required for travelling abroad.

It further observed that there was no legal basis for mentioning an FIR in a character certificate after the proceedings had culminated in a final acquittal. Any certificate containing such a reference would be legally invalid.

Justice Ayyaz Shaukat also rejected the police’s description of the petitioner as having been “discharged” during the investigation, observing that such a characterisation undermined the legal effect and status of the acquittal.

The court held that including an FIR in a character certificate despite an individual’s acquittal violated Articles 4, 9, 14 and 15 of the Constitution, which protect citizens’ rights, liberty, dignity and freedom of movement.

It emphasised that a person acquitted through due process of law could not continue to face adverse consequences through a character certificate suggesting involvement in criminal proceedings.

The court directed the Islamabad police chief to introduce a proper procedure to ensure that acquitted citizens did not have to initiate fresh litigation merely to obtain character certificates reflecting their actual legal status.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: Phantom Blade Zero debuts strongly
ECP begins registration of voters in Punjab's Kasur, Sindh's Qamber-Shahdadkot
description: The initiative aims to identify women eligible for CNICs and voter registration, encourage them to register and facilitate the process.
author: Iftikhar A. Khan
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Saturday announced a pilot project to reduce the gender gap in voter registration in Kasur district of Punjab and Qamber-Shahdadkot district of Sindh.

According to the ECP, data collection for the initiative will be carried out in November 2026, while voter registration activities will continue from December 2026 to February 2027.

The initiative aims to identify women eligible for Computerised National Identity Cards (CNICs) and voter registration, encourage them to register and facilitate the process.

Local social workers and enumerators will conduct door-to-door visits to prepare statistical block-wise lists and run awareness campaigns. The National Database and Registration Authority’s (Nadra) Mobile Registration Vans (MRVs) will be deployed at their doorsteps, while facilitation will also be provided at registration centres established in government buildings.

Through the campaign, the ECP aims to facilitate the registration of 115,689 women in Kasur and 59,156 in Qamber-Shah­dadkot. Areas with a wider gender gap will be prioritised in the initial phase.

Representatives of the education and health sectors, civil society organisations and local communities will assist the ECP in the initiative.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: Uncertain local governments
description: The ECP is battling both the federal and provincial governments that are reluctant to hold LG polls.
author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob
article_text:
THE battle between the Election Commission of Pakistan and the provincial and federal governments has been an almost permanent feature of Pakistan’s electoral scene since 2010, when the responsibility for holding local government elections was entrusted to the Commission under the 18th Amendment.

Currently, the ECP is fighting a four-way battle — with the provincial governments of Punjab and KP, the federal government, and the cantonment boards — for LG elections in the two provinces, Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT), and the cantonment boards.

The LGs in Sindh and Balochistan (except in the largest district of Quetta, where the entire term passed without election) have yet to complete their terms.

The ICT LG election is the most disappointing case. The last LG election in ICT was held in November 2015. Its five-year term ended on Feb 14, 2021.

Under the Elections Act, 2017, the new election was to take place within 120 days after the previous LGs’ term ended, making June 15, 2021, the due date for the next election.

For more than five years, the ECP and the federal government have been haggling over legal points and the possible date of the next election. Since 2021, the ECP has issued the election schedule four times and carried out fresh delimitation five times. Each time it has had to eat humble pie by withdrawing the schedule as the federal government changed the goalposts and amended the LG election law.

The latest in the series was the ICT Local Government (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, promulgated on Jan 10, 2026, which drastically changed the capital’s LG system. However, the ordinance lapsed in September 2026.

While parliament is going through the motions of converting the lapsed ordinance into an act of parliament, the ECP maintains that the old ICTLGA, 2015, stands resurrected after the ordinance lapsed and, therefore, issued a polling schedule on Oct 25, fixing Dec 20 as polling day.

Looking back at the federal government’s track record, the new act is likely to pass in the next few days, after which the ECP would have no choice but to withdraw the schedule and begin preparations anew.

The case of KP is not very different; the terms of the LGs expired on June 19, 2026, after which new elections should have taken place by Oct 20, but the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local Government (Amendment) Act, 2026,was passedand became effective on July 16 this year. It changed the size of the village and neighbourhood councils. The ECP strongly objected to the amendment, termed it a delaying tactic, and asked the provincial government to review the law.

In the meantime, the ECP is proceeding with preparations to hold the LG polls, except in 12 districts where the law and order situation doesn’t permit polls. The ECP has yet to issue an election schedule. Still, it remains to be seen whether the National Assembly, which has the legislative powers of the KP Assembly after the proclamation of emergency, will amend the LG law or whether the elections will be postponed yet again on some pretext or the other.

All formalities for holding the LG election in Punjab have been completed by the ECP and the Punjab government under the Punjab Local Government Act, 2025. If finally held, this will be the first LG election in roughly 11 years.

The election was supposed to be held in May 2022, but a series of new laws and amendments kept postponing it. Although the Punjab government ministerial committee and the ECP agreed to hold the election in three phases between Dec 15 and Jan 15, the Punjab government changed its mind and asked the ECP to defer the election until April 2027 because of dense fog and school exams in December. The ECP immediately rejected the new dates and asked its secretariat to prepare an election schedule based on the earlier agreed dates. The election schedule has not yet been issued; one should wait to see which side blinks first.

The election to 43 cantonment boards in the country was due on Aug 8 as the four-year term of the previously elected boards expired on April 11, 2026. The cantonment boards’ election has an additional prerequisite: the ECP should receive the federal government’s request before holding the election. Reportedly, no such request has been received, and the ECP, given the legal requirement to hold elections within 120 days of the expiry of the term, is trying to reach out to the federal government. Regardless of the outcome of these efforts, the election to the cantonment boards is also overdue.

These four stories lead to a single conclusion: both the federal and provincial governments are reluctant to hold LG elections on one pretext or another.

The key flaw in the system is that while the ECP is responsible for holding LG elections, the governments and their legislatures alone write the LG laws. There is no bar on legislatures amending LG laws. As demonstrated repeatedly, the law can be amended after the announcement of the election schedule and even a few days before polling day, undoing all the preparation made by the ECP such as delimiting LG boundaries.

The solution is for parliament to amend the Elections Act, 2017, and bar any amendment to the LG laws after the expiry of the LG term, so the ECP can prepare unimpeded and hold timely elections.

As if these difficulties were not enough to make the future of LGs uncertain, another layer of unpredictability has been added by the possibility of carving out new provinces and, in the case of ICT, by the announcement that Islamabad may soon have provincial status. This may give the government yet another pretext to slow-walk LG elections.

THE battle between the Election Commission of Pakistan and the provincial and federal governments has been an almost permanent feature of Pakistan’s electoral scene since 2010, when the responsibility for holding local government elections was entrusted to the Commission under the 18th Amendment.

Currently, the ECP is fighting a four-way battle — with the provincial governments of Punjab and KP, the federal government, and the cantonment boards — for LG elections in the two provinces, Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT), and the cantonment boards.

The LGs in Sindh and Balochistan (except in the largest district of Quetta, where the entire term passed without election) have yet to complete their terms.

The ICT LG election is the most disappointing case. The last LG election in ICT was held in November 2015. Its five-year term ended on Feb 14, 2021.

Under the Elections Act, 2017, the new election was to take place within 120 days after the previous LGs’ term ended, making June 15, 2021, the due date for the next election.

For more than five years, the ECP and the federal government have been haggling over legal points and the possible date of the next election. Since 2021, the ECP has issued the election schedule four times and carried out fresh delimitation five times. Each time it has had to eat humble pie by withdrawing the schedule as the federal government changed the goalposts and amended the LG election law.

The latest in the series was the ICT Local Government (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, promulgated on Jan 10, 2026, which drastically changed the capital’s LG system. However, the ordinance lapsed in September 2026.

While parliament is going through the motions of converting the lapsed ordinance into an act of parliament, the ECP maintains that the old ICTLGA, 2015, stands resurrected after the ordinance lapsed and, therefore, issued a polling schedule on Oct 25, fixing Dec 20 as polling day.

Looking back at the federal government’s track record, the new act is likely to pass in the next few days, after which the ECP would have no choice but to withdraw the schedule and begin preparations anew.

The case of KP is not very different; the terms of the LGs expired on June 19, 2026, after which new elections should have taken place by Oct 20, but the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local Government (Amendment) Act, 2026,was passedand became effective on July 16 this year. It changed the size of the village and neighbourhood councils. The ECP strongly objected to the amendment, termed it a delaying tactic, and asked the provincial government to review the law.

In the meantime, the ECP is proceeding with preparations to hold the LG polls, except in 12 districts where the law and order situation doesn’t permit polls. The ECP has yet to issue an election schedule. Still, it remains to be seen whether the National Assembly, which has the legislative powers of the KP Assembly after the proclamation of emergency, will amend the LG law or whether the elections will be postponed yet again on some pretext or the other.

The ECP is battling both the federal and provincial governments that are reluctant to hold LG polls.

All formalities for holding the LG election in Punjab have been completed by the ECP and the Punjab government under the Punjab Local Government Act, 2025. If finally held, this will be the first LG election in roughly 11 years.

The election was supposed to be held in May 2022, but a series of new laws and amendments kept postponing it. Although the Punjab government ministerial committee and the ECP agreed to hold the election in three phases between Dec 15 and Jan 15, the Punjab government changed its mind and asked the ECP to defer the election until April 2027 because of dense fog and school exams in December. The ECP immediately rejected the new dates and asked its secretariat to prepare an election schedule based on the earlier agreed dates. The election schedule has not yet been issued; one should wait to see which side blinks first.

The election to 43 cantonment boards in the country was due on Aug 8 as the four-year term of the previously elected boards expired on April 11, 2026. The cantonment boards’ election has an additional prerequisite: the ECP should receive the federal government’s request before holding the election. Reportedly, no such request has been received, and the ECP, given the legal requirement to hold elections within 120 days of the expiry of the term, is trying to reach out to the federal government. Regardless of the outcome of these efforts, the election to the cantonment boards is also overdue.

These four stories lead to a single conclusion: both the federal and provincial governments are reluctant to hold LG elections on one pretext or another.

The key flaw in the system is that while the ECP is responsible for holding LG elections, the governments and their legislatures alone write the LG laws. There is no bar on legislatures amending LG laws. As demonstrated repeatedly, the law can be amended after the announcement of the election schedule and even a few days before polling day, undoing all the preparation made by the ECP such as delimiting LG boundaries.

The solution is for parliament to amend the Elections Act, 2017, and bar any amendment to the LG laws after the expiry of the LG term, so the ECP can prepare unimpeded and hold timely elections.

As if these difficulties were not enough to make the future of LGs uncertain, another layer of unpredictability has been added by the possibility of carving out new provinces and, in the case of ICT, by the announcement that Islamabad may soon have provincial status. This may give the government yet another pretext to slow-walk LG elections.

headline: CM Bugti stresses dialogue to resolve Balochistan issues
description: Says certain quartersare spreading confusion and misleading narratives in the name of highlighting Balochistan’s grievances and the genuine problems of its people.
author: Saleem Shahid
article_text:
QUETTA: Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti has said there is no justification for violence on the basis of a sense of deprivation or political disagreement, stressing that the province’s problems can only be resolved through education, dialogue, political engagement and democratic practices.

Speaking at the convocation ceremony of the University of Management and Technology (UMT) in Lahore on Saturday, he said, “Our loyalty to Pakistan is unconditional.” He added that the people of Balochistan were equal citizens of the country and that their genuine grievances, development needs and sense of deprivation must be properly understood and addressed.

CM Bugti said Balochistan was currently facing three major challenges: narratives seeking to justify violence, armed terrorism and attempts to influence the thinking of young people through social media.

He said certain quarters were spreading confusion and misleading narratives in the name of highlighting Balochistan’s grievances and the genuine problems of its people. He stressed that issues such as poverty, underdevelopment and deprivation should not be used to justify or support separatist violence.

headline: Retired officials call for respecting people’s wishes
description: Seek equal treatment of provinces, warn against constitutional changes imposed against public will.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: A group of retired civil servants, diplomats and military generals has called for equal treatment of all provinces and warned against any constitutional amendment imposed against the wishes of the people, saying the country’s unity and future were at risk amid a deepening political and economic crisis.

In a statement shared with Dawn on Saturday, the Roedad Khan Club, often described as Islamabad’s ‘retired establishment’ because it comprises retired but influential officials, said constitutional rule must be restored in practice rather than maintained as a facade.

The statement was signed by former air chief retired Air Chief Marshal Abbas Khattak, former bureaucrat Shakil Durrani and former diplomats Ashraf Jehangir Qazi, Humayun Qazi and Asif Durrani.

Seek equal treatment of provinces, warn against constitutional changes imposed against public will

“Constitutional rule needs to be restored as a reality, and not as a facade. The military needs to return to its sacred mission of protecting the country, its oath of allegiance, and [Quaid-i-Azam Moha­mmad Ali Jinnah’s] clear instructions,” it said.

The statement comes amid renewed debate over restructuring the provincial system following proposals by senior government figures for the creation of new provinces. The proposals have drawn opposition from political quarters concerned that changes to the provincial map could undermine provincial autonomy and alter the existing balance of power.

The club also rejected what it described as hybrid governance, arguing that a system “in which elected civilian institutions operate alongside an unelected centre of power deepens political resentment and undermines constitutional rule”.

It called for a return to the electoral mandate, saying this could provide a basis for national reconciliation and political stability.

“What is required, instead, is a restitution of the people’s verdict in the last general elections. Alternatively, a fresh election with all the national and regional parties and their chosen leaders participating needs to be a first step on a journey of national reconciliation, revival, transformation and prosperity,” it added.

headline: India’s water blackmail
description: For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic.
author: Khurram Abbas
article_text:
SINCE April 2025, when India unilaterally suspended the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), most scholarship has treated it as a political decision by the BJP-led NDA government. While it is true that the BJP has been developing a narrative that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi was ‘rectifying’ the ‘mistakes’ of the Nehruvian era, the decisions and developments during the past 18 months suggest that New Delhi is developing a long-term strategy to strangle Pakistan economically.

India’s primary target in this strategic campaign is the Chenab river, which it is systematically converting into a long-term instrument of leverage to dictate Pakistan’s foreign policy, weaken its stance on Kashmir, and dominate bilateral relations.

In the 18 months since it decided to keep the IWT in abeyance, India has aggressively leveraged this treaty vacuum to build a massive network of storage, regulation, and diversion infrastructure on the Chenab. New and accelerated hydroelectric power projects, primarily concentrated in the Chenab basin, have ballooned from a baseline capacity of 3,263 MW to 7,620.5 MW, supported by a massive financial outlay of approximately Indian rupees 414.04 billion.

No single dam or diversion canal can permanently dry up a river. However, a highly synchronised, connected network of mega structures, coupled with diversion canals, can fundamentally determine who controls the timing and volume of river flow.

India is trying to apply a two-pronged strategy, ie, increase storage capacity and enhance the ability to divert the Chenab’s water. India’s strategic roadmap involves five megaprojects alongside extensive local diversions. This includes Sawalkot (1,856 MW), Kirthai I & II (1,320 MW), Pakal Dul (1,000 MW), Ratle (850 MW), and Bursar Storage (800 MW).

India’s infrastructure push began in May 2025, with the announcement of the tender for the Uri-II project (240 MW), followed quickly in June 2025 by the tender announcement for the Dulhasti-II project (260 MW). Activity accelerated in July 2025 with two major announcements — first, a tender for the removal of deposited sediments from the Salal Dam Reservoir, and second, the Sawalkot project (1,856 MW) tender under international competitive bidding. In March 2026, civil contracts were officially awarded for both the Uri-I stage II and Dulhasti stage-II projects, alongside the official tender announcement for the highly controversial Chenab-Beas Link Tunnel Project (Link-3). These aforementioned projects command a combined potential diversion and storage capacity of roughly 7.287 MAF.

For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations.

The Chenab-Beas Link Project is particularly consequential. With a reported budget of Indian rupees 23.52bn, it proposes to transfer water from the Chandra river, a major Chenab tributary, through an 8.7-kilometre tunnel into the Beas basin and onward through a 113km canal network to eastern Indian states. The proposed diversion of 1.9 MAF annually from the Chenab basin raises serious questions about compliance with Article III of the IWT.

The threat of manipulation, or the Chenab’s vulnerabilities, poses a direct risk to Pakistan’s economic survival, social stability, and national security. The Chenab directly irrigates agricultural lands across more than 11 districts of central Punjab, the country’s undisputed food basket. These districts form the densest core of the famous rice-wheat cropping zone. This 11-district area accounts for about 22 to 25 per cent of Pakistan’s national food grain output. If India controls water flows during October to December or May to July, it may affect seasonal yields in this zone. In such a scenario, it could cause a direct blow of $9bn to $11bn to Pakistan’s economy.

The broader impact would ripple through the national economy in several ways. Pakistan would be forced to spend billions of scarce foreign exchange reserves to import basic food commodities. Instead of generating $3.3bn to $4bn from booming rice exports, the country would face a multibillion-dollar trade deficit just trying to secure alternative grain imports. Second, any sustained restriction on, or unpredictable disruption to, these water flows would threaten the livelihoods of millions of farming households, while endangering crops and compromising national food security.

Therefore, Islamabad must view India’s decision to place the IWT in abeyance as another dimension of New Delhi’s long-standing and coordinated policy of economic strangulation of Pakistan. For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations.

New Delhi has been consistently trying to restrict Islamabad’s access to global capital and limit its trade capacity. A primary example is India’s aggressive lobbying within the Financial Action Task Force, where it has consistently tried to politicise technical compliance and block Pakistan’s removal from the grey list to discourage foreign direct investment and cripple its banking sector. Beyond regulatory warfare, India has systematically disrupted regional trade platforms, such as Saarc, effectively stalling economic integration across South Asia to keep Pakistan regionally isolated.

Faced with this asymmetric threat, Islamabad’s response has been largely concentrated on the external front. Pakistan’s state apparatus has consistently pursued international legal and diplomatic channels.

However, a dangerous policy gap exists on the domestic front. Ground-level preparedness is profoundly lacking. The agrarian communities, provincial irrigation departments, and economic sectors that will bear the immediate impact of India’s upstream infrastructure remain highly vulnerable. Pakistan lacks the modern water-storage infrastructure, optimised canal lining, crop-switching strategies, and real-time early warning systems needed to survive sudden changes in river flows.

Hence, Islamabad should complement its legal and diplomatic efforts with urgent domestic reforms. Pakistan must declare a national water emergency, educate vulnerable communities in 11 districts of central Punjab that depend on the Chenab, expedite dam construction, and modernise irrigation. Without urgent preparedness, Islamabad will risk surrendering its agricultural security to Delhi’s water blackmail.

The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.

article_html:
SINCE April 2025, when India unilaterally suspended the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), most scholarship has treated it as a political decision by the BJP-led NDA government. While it is true that the BJP has been developing a narrative that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi was ‘rectifying’ the ‘mistakes’ of the Nehruvian era, the decisions and developments during the past 18 months suggest that New Delhi is developing a long-term strategy to strangle Pakistan economically.

India’s primary target in this strategic campaign is the Chenab river, which it is systematically converting into a long-term instrument of leverage to dictate Pakistan’s foreign policy, weaken its stance on Kashmir, and dominate bilateral relations.

In the 18 months since it decided to keep the IWT in abeyance, India has aggressively leveraged this treaty vacuum to build a massive network of storage, regulation, and diversion infrastructure on the Chenab. New and accelerated hydroelectric power projects, primarily concentrated in the Chenab basin, have ballooned from a baseline capacity of 3,263 MW to 7,620.5 MW, supported by a massive financial outlay of approximately Indian rupees 414.04 billion.

No single dam or diversion canal can permanently dry up a river. However, a highly synchronised, connected network of mega structures, coupled with diversion canals, can fundamentally determine who controls the timing and volume of river flow.

India is trying to apply a two-pronged strategy, ie, increase storage capacity and enhance the ability to divert the Chenab’s water. India’s strategic roadmap involves five megaprojects alongside extensive local diversions. This includes Sawalkot (1,856 MW), Kirthai I & II (1,320 MW), Pakal Dul (1,000 MW), Ratle (850 MW), and Bursar Storage (800 MW).

India’s infrastructure push began in May 2025, with the announcement of the tender for the Uri-II project (240 MW), followed quickly in June 2025 by the tender announcement for the Dulhasti-II project (260 MW). Activity accelerated in July 2025 with two major announcements — first, a tender for the removal of deposited sediments from the Salal Dam Reservoir, and second, the Sawalkot project (1,856 MW) tender under international competitive bidding. In March 2026, civil contracts were officially awarded for both the Uri-I stage II and Dulhasti stage-II projects, alongside the official tender announcement for the highly controversial Chenab-Beas Link Tunnel Project (Link-3). These aforementioned projects command a combined potential diversion and storage capacity of roughly 7.287 MAF.

For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations.

The Chenab-Beas Link Project is particularly consequential. With a reported budget of Indian rupees 23.52bn, it proposes to transfer water from the Chandra river, a major Chenab tributary, through an 8.7-kilometre tunnel into the Beas basin and onward through a 113km canal network to eastern Indian states. The proposed diversion of 1.9 MAF annually from the Chenab basin raises serious questions about compliance with Article III of the IWT.

The threat of manipulation, or the Chenab’s vulnerabilities, poses a direct risk to Pakistan’s economic survival, social stability, and national security. The Chenab directly irrigates agricultural lands across more than 11 districts of central Punjab, the country’s undisputed food basket. These districts form the densest core of the famous rice-wheat cropping zone. This 11-district area accounts for about 22 to 25 per cent of Pakistan’s national food grain output. If India controls water flows during October to December or May to July, it may affect seasonal yields in this zone. In such a scenario, it could cause a direct blow of $9bn to $11bn to Pakistan’s economy.

The broader impact would ripple through the national economy in several ways. Pakistan would be forced to spend billions of scarce foreign exchange reserves to import basic food commodities. Instead of generating $3.3bn to $4bn from booming rice exports, the country would face a multibillion-dollar trade deficit just trying to secure alternative grain imports. Second, any sustained restriction on, or unpredictable disruption to, these water flows would threaten the livelihoods of millions of farming households, while endangering crops and compromising national food security.

Therefore, Islamabad must view India’s decision to place the IWT in abeyance as another dimension of New Delhi’s long-standing and coordinated policy of economic strangulation of Pakistan. For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations.

New Delhi has been consistently trying to restrict Islamabad’s access to global capital and limit its trade capacity. A primary example is India’s aggressive lobbying within the Financial Action Task Force, where it has consistently tried to politicise technical compliance and block Pakistan’s removal from the grey list to discourage foreign direct investment and cripple its banking sector. Beyond regulatory warfare, India has systematically disrupted regional trade platforms, such as Saarc, effectively stalling economic integration across South Asia to keep Pakistan regionally isolated.

Faced with this asymmetric threat, Islamabad’s response has been largely concentrated on the external front. Pakistan’s state apparatus has consistently pursued international legal and diplomatic channels.

However, a dangerous policy gap exists on the domestic front. Ground-level preparedness is profoundly lacking. The agrarian communities, provincial irrigation departments, and economic sectors that will bear the immediate impact of India’s upstream infrastructure remain highly vulnerable. Pakistan lacks the modern water-storage infrastructure, optimised canal lining, crop-switching strategies, and real-time early warning systems needed to survive sudden changes in river flows.

Hence, Islamabad should complement its legal and diplomatic efforts with urgent domestic reforms. Pakistan must declare a national water emergency, educate vulnerable communities in 11 districts of central Punjab that depend on the Chenab, expedite dam construction, and modernise irrigation. Without urgent preparedness, Islamabad will risk surrendering its agricultural security to Delhi’s water blackmail.

The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: Consumer firms defy economic headwinds
description: Local and multinational companies post robust sales growth this year.
author: Aamir Shafaat Khan
article_text:
KARACHI: Amid rising food inflation and weakening purchasing power from higher fuel costs driven by Middle East tensions since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on Feb 28, local and multinational consumer goods companies in Pakistan reported improved sales in the first nine months of 2026 and the first quarter of FY27.

However, some companies remain cautious about their full-year 2026 outlook amid persistent inflationary pressures.

Nestlé Pakistan

Nestlé Pakistan’s net sales for the nine months ended Sept 30, amounted to Rs160bn, up 6.3pc from the corresponding period last year.

Despite rising inflation, political instability and higher fuel and energy prices amid the US-Iran war, the company sustained its business momentum. It attributed its performance to increased investment in brands, product innovation and renovation (I&R), stronger marketplace execution, improved export channels and disciplined pricing, where necessary.

Local and multinational companies post robust sales growth this year

Net profit after tax rose 3.1pc to Rs14.526bn from Rs14.1bn a year earlier, despite higher tax expenses. In response to geopolitical uncertainty, the company accelerated localisation and secured essential inventories to reduce foreign exchange exposure, strengthen supply chain resilience and ensure uninterrupted operations.

Citing geopolitical instability, volatile energy and input costs, and persistent inflation, Nestlé maintained a cautious outlook for 2026.

FrieslandCampina Engro Pakistan

FrieslandCampina Engro Pakistan’s revenue increased 10.1pc to Rs88.4bn in the first nine months of 2026 from Rs80.2bn in the corresponding period last year. The company attributed the growth to a favourable product mix, stronger market execution and selective investment in brands. Profit rose to Rs6.5bn from Rs2bn a year earlier.

Regional conflicts, higher freight and energy prices put pressure on the company’s operations and input costs during the third quarter of 2026. In Pakistan, inflation and interest rates also constrained household purchasing power, affecting product affordability and demand, the company said.

Unilever Pakistan

Unilever Pakistan Foods’ sales rose to Rs37.6bn in the first nine months of 2026 from Rs30bn a year earlier, while profit after tax increased to Rs6.326bn from Rs4.6bn.

Unilever said Pakistan’s economy remained resilient, supported by higher foreign exchange reserves, fiscal consolidation and a gradual recovery in economic activity. However, renewed inflation, higher global commodity and energy prices, and Middle East tensions continued to constrain consumer spending, the company added.

Colgate-Palmolive Pakistan

Colgate-Palmolive Pakistan’s sales rose 25.53pc to Rs52.7bn in July-September 2026, driven by higher prices and sales volumes. Profit after tax increased 8pc to Rs4.9bn compared with the corresponding period last year.

The company said persistent inflation, tax collection constraints and high energy tariffs continued to pose challenges. Regional tensions also posed supply chain risks because of its reliance on Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries for essential raw materials.

Fauji Foods

Fauji Foods Limited (FFL) recorded its highest-ever nine-month revenue of Rs23.9bn in 2026, up 14.1pc from the corresponding period last year. However, profit after tax fell to Rs666m from Rs945m. Despite inflationary pressures on consumption, FFL reported growth across its product portfolio.

National Foods Limited

National Foods Limited’s sales rose to Rs11.1bn in July-September 2026 from Rs10bn a year earlier, while profit increased to Rs888m from Rs801m.

According to Rabia Yousuf of Topline Securities, National Foods informed shareholders at its 55th annual general meeting, held recently, that it expected revenue growth of 15pc in FY27, with scope for further improvement if macroeconomic conditions improved.

She said management highlighted a rise in freight rates from $500-$600 to $5,000 per container. Continuing tensions in the Middle East may also constrain export volume growth.

Management plans to launch more than 25 products and remains optimistic about expanding its portfolio.

However, some companies remain cautious about their full-year 2026 outlook amid persistent inflationary pressures.

Nestlé Pakistan

Nestlé Pakistan’s net sales for the nine months ended Sept 30, amounted to Rs160bn, up 6.3pc from the corresponding period last year.

Despite rising inflation, political instability and higher fuel and energy prices amid the US-Iran war, the company sustained its business momentum. It attributed its performance to increased investment in brands, product innovation and renovation (I&R), stronger marketplace execution, improved export channels and disciplined pricing, where necessary.

Local and multinational companies post robust sales growth this year

Net profit after tax rose 3.1pc to Rs14.526bn from Rs14.1bn a year earlier, despite higher tax expenses. In response to geopolitical uncertainty, the company accelerated localisation and secured essential inventories to reduce foreign exchange exposure, strengthen supply chain resilience and ensure uninterrupted operations.

Citing geopolitical instability, volatile energy and input costs, and persistent inflation, Nestlé maintained a cautious outlook for 2026.

FrieslandCampina Engro Pakistan

FrieslandCampina Engro Pakistan’s revenue increased 10.1pc to Rs88.4bn in the first nine months of 2026 from Rs80.2bn in the corresponding period last year. The company attributed the growth to a favourable product mix, stronger market execution and selective investment in brands. Profit rose to Rs6.5bn from Rs2bn a year earlier.

Regional conflicts, higher freight and energy prices put pressure on the company’s operations and input costs during the third quarter of 2026. In Pakistan, inflation and interest rates also constrained household purchasing power, affecting product affordability and demand, the company said.

Unilever Pakistan

Unilever Pakistan Foods’ sales rose to Rs37.6bn in the first nine months of 2026 from Rs30bn a year earlier, while profit after tax increased to Rs6.326bn from Rs4.6bn.

Unilever said Pakistan’s economy remained resilient, supported by higher foreign exchange reserves, fiscal consolidation and a gradual recovery in economic activity. However, renewed inflation, higher global commodity and energy prices, and Middle East tensions continued to constrain consumer spending, the company added.

Colgate-Palmolive Pakistan

Colgate-Palmolive Pakistan’s sales rose 25.53pc to Rs52.7bn in July-September 2026, driven by higher prices and sales volumes. Profit after tax increased 8pc to Rs4.9bn compared with the corresponding period last year.

The company said persistent inflation, tax collection constraints and high energy tariffs continued to pose challenges. Regional tensions also posed supply chain risks because of its reliance on Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries for essential raw materials.

Fauji Foods

Fauji Foods Limited (FFL) recorded its highest-ever nine-month revenue of Rs23.9bn in 2026, up 14.1pc from the corresponding period last year. However, profit after tax fell to Rs666m from Rs945m. Despite inflationary pressures on consumption, FFL reported growth across its product portfolio.

National Foods Limited

National Foods Limited’s sales rose to Rs11.1bn in July-September 2026 from Rs10bn a year earlier, while profit increased to Rs888m from Rs801m.

According to Rabia Yousuf of Topline Securities, National Foods informed shareholders at its 55th annual general meeting, held recently, that it expected revenue growth of 15pc in FY27, with scope for further improvement if macroeconomic conditions improved.

She said management highlighted a rise in freight rates from $500-$600 to $5,000 per container. Continuing tensions in the Middle East may also constrain export volume growth.

Management plans to launch more than 25 products and remains optimistic about expanding its portfolio.

headline: ‘Medicine pricing needs serious attention’
description: Pharmaceutical industries seek an increase in medicine prices, but the matter is under consideration by the federal cabinet.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
KARACHI: More than 86,000 medicines produced by pharmaceutical companies have been registered under the Track and Trace System, allowing consumers to scan products by mobile phone to check their authenticity and find out their prices, Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal said.

He said that pharmaceutical companies could also register their medicines and products online. A process that previously took years is now being completed within just 21 days.

Addressing the members of the Korangi Association of Trade and Industry (KATI) on Saturday, he said the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) has been made fully transparent and digitalised.

Eight months had passed since DRAP’s certification procedures were shifted to a digital system, during which more than 5,000 cases had been processed, he said.

Mustafa Kamal said the issue of medicine pricing requires serious attention. The pharmaceutical industries seek an increase in medicine prices, but the matter is under consideration by the federal cabinet.

The issue has two dimensions as an increase in medicine prices will create additional financial difficulties for ordinary citizens, while keeping prices unchanged could lead to shortages of medicines for serious illnesses. Consequently, patients were sometimes forced to purchase the same medicines from the black market at three times their actual price.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026
