headline: PTI seeks extension in Islamabad LG polls nomination deadline
description: Party's Islamabad president alleges candidates unable to obtain nomination papers.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) Islamabad chapter has demanded that the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) should extend the deadline for submission of nomination papers for the upcoming local government elections in the capital by at least 10 days.

PTI Islamabad president and core committee member Amir Mughal, while talking to Dawn, alleged that candidates were unable to obtain nomination papers on Friday despite the schedule issued by the ECP for the elections in 125 union councils.

He claimed that no staff was present at the offices of returning officers. He said watchmen at some schools and offices told candidates that the nomination papers would be available on Monday.

Mr Mughal demanded an immediate extension of at least 10 days in the nomination-paper submission schedule, saying candidates should be given sufficient time to obtain, complete and submit the forms. He also questioned the conduct of the local elections, alleging that the government and the ECP were preparing to delay or avoid the polls for the fifth time.

The PTI leader criticised the legal framework under which the Islamabad local elections were being held, claiming that elected local representatives would have limited authority while major powers would remain with the bureaucracy.

He also alleged that the same Election Commission leadership was overseeing the local elections that had conducted the 2024 general elections, which he said were rigged.

Mr Mughal said PTI had decided to contest the elections after consultations with different party organisations. He claimed that more than 25 meetings had been held over the past three days, involving more than 400 office-bearers.

He also claimed that residents facing displacement from their ancestral land and homes, as well as people living in informal settlements, would express their grievances through the ballot.

He said Islamabad had traditionally been a stronghold of PTI and expressed confidence that the party would perform strongly in the local elections.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: Double murder suspects killed in CCD shootout in Attock
description: Police claim the suspects were killed by their own accomplices during an exchange of fire.
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
TAXILA: Two suspects allegedly belonging to the Odh gang involved in a double murder were killed in a shootout with the Crime Control Department (CCD) in Attock, officials said on Saturday.

A police spokesperson claimed that the suspects were killed by their own accomplices during an exchange of fire near Bota village on Bhattiyot Road.

The deceased were identified as Haq Nawaz alias Haqoo, described by police as the alleged mastermind and head of the Odh gang, and Saleem alias Sheem. Two .30-bore pistols were reportedly recovered from their possession.

Police said the suspects were wanted in connection with the abduction and murder of two persons in Fatehjang, including 11-year-old Saim Raza, who was reportedly taken from Vehari, and an unidentified mentally disabled man abducted from the Rawat area along G.T. Road on Sept 24.

According to investigators, the victims were allegedly killed with axes and sticks, and their bodies disfigured to conceal their identities. Police further claimed that the suspects had posed as relatives of the victims and lodged a false case against their rivals, accusing them of abducting his daughter for sexual exploitation.

The investigation by Fatehjang police reportedly exposed the alleged double murder and identified the complainants as the main suspects.

headline: Federal prison law draft sent to interior ministry for approval
description: Proposed legislation provides for prisoners’ rights, welfare and rehabilitation.
author: Munawer Azeem
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: A final draft of the Federal Prison and Correctional Facility Act, 2026, has been prepared and sent to the Ministry of Interior for approval before its introduction and implementation in the federal capital.

The proposed legislation seeks to provide a legal framework for prisons, the reformation of prisoners and their rehabilitation.

Officials familiar with the matter told Dawn that the Act was being drafted to provide for the establishment, management, safety and security of prisons, the care and custody of prisoners, their reformation and rehabilitation, and related matters. The final draft of the Federal Prison and Correctional Facility Act, 2026, was prepared by newly appointed Senior Superintendent of Prison Ali Akbar.

According to the proposed draft, the objectives of the Federal Prison System include contributing to the maintenance and protection of a just, peaceful and safe society by enforcing sentences awarded by courts, the Act and its regulations in the prescribed manner.

Proposed legislation provides for prisoners’ rights, welfare and rehabilitation

These objectives also include keeping prisoners in safe and secure custody, ensuring the implementation of their fundamental rights as enshrined in the Constitution, relevant international conventions to which Pakistan is a party, and applicable laws, without compromising the objectives of punishment and correctional measures. The system also aims to promote prisoners’ welfare and rehabilitation and their reintegration into society as law-abiding citizens by adopting best practices.

Basic principles for dealing with prisoners include that every prisoner shall accept the authority of prison officers and obey their lawful instructions.

All prisoners shall be treated with due respect, recognising their inherent dignity and worth as human beings. All sentenced prisoners shall participate in the reformation process and ensure its implementation.

They may be offered incentives in the form of special remissions and monetary benefits, as may be prescribed. There shall be no discrimination on any basis except as provided under the law.

The government may declare any building, enclosure, land or premises to be a Federal Prison and Correctional Facility for the purposes of the Act.

The government may establish, alter, expand or relocate any prison; specify its classification or category; declare that any prison shall cease to function as a prison from a specified date; and direct the removal and transfer of prisoners to another prison specified in the notification.

It may also declare any place to be a subsidiary or temporary prison for the reception or detention of prisoners. Every prison declared under the Act shall be subject to the administrative control and management of the Inspector General.

A Prison Management Board, headed by the chief commissioner and comprising other members, shall be established.

The board shall make recommendations for the efficient and transparent management of prisons to ensure the highest level of public service for prisoners.

It shall also establish an Oversight Committee for prisoners’ welfare, philanthropic initiatives, rehabilitation programmes, monitoring of prison administration or any other related purpose.

Prison officers shall be provided with weapons, uniforms, equipment and other accoutrements.

As per the draft, a prison officer found guilty of misconduct shall be liable to the prescribed penalty following disciplinary proceedings. The officer shall have at least one right of appeal.

Every prisoner shall remain in the lawful custody of a prison officer during the period of imprisonment and shall comply with prison discipline, the Act and the rules. Prisoners shall be informed of their duties, rights and obligations, which may also be published. They shall also undergo medical and psychological examinations as prescribed under the rules.

Prisoners shall be allowed to lodge complaints freely, and a mechanism based on modern standards shall be established to address them. Technologies shall also be adopted and integrated to enhance operational efficiency, accountability, security and discipline within the prison system.

Prisoners may personally send and receive letters and make or receive audio and video calls through facilities provided in the prison. Relatives, friends or persons providing legal assistance may visit prisoners.

They may also receive their spouses for the exercise of conjugal rights. All correspondence, communications and visits shall be supervised by a prison officer, as may be prescribed.

The SSP may initiate necessary action against a prisoner found involved in a breach of discipline or a criminal offence under any law.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: In Spectrum: Gymkhana: colonial origins and politics of selective outrage
description: Institutions, like societies, can evolve, and their ability to transcend the circumstances of their creation is an important measure of historical adaptation.
author: Tahir Kamran
article_text:
The British did not establish clubs in colonial India merely for cricket, golf and other recreations. They formed part of the social architecture of colonial rule, providing civil and military officials with spaces to cultivate networks, consolidate solidarity and preserve racial distinctions.

The exclusion of Indians from establishments reserved for Europeans reflected the belief that political domination conferred social superiority. This history deserves unequivocal condemnation.

Yet condemning an institution’s colonial origins does not automatically invalidate its subsequent existence. Institutions, like societies, can evolve, and their ability to transcend the circumstances of their creation is an important measure of historical adaptation.

Lahore Gymkhana emerged from this world of colonial exclusivity and acquired its present name on March 23, 1906. Its history, however, cannot be frozen at the moment of its inception. Partition in 1947 dismantled the political and social order that had sustained colonial institutions, yet Lahore Gymkhana survived and gradually became part of the civilian life of ‘independent’ Pakistan.

An institution originally designed for a privileged foreign establishment adapted to a different national and social environment, drawing members from professional, business and salaried circles. While it remains selective and cannot be described as wholly egalitarian, its contemporary identity is no longer synonymous with the racial exclusivity of its founders.

It should be borne in mind that salaried individuals are among those whose incomes are taxed at source, and the revenue generated through taxation helps meet government expenditures without relying solely on loans from international institutions. Those crying foul over Gymkhana are privileged individuals who, in many cases, do not bear their fair share of the tax burden.

Anyhow reverting to the transformation deserves recognition, particularly in a country where many inherited institutions changed their personnel after independence without fundamentally altering their hierarchical structures.

Lahore Gymkhana’s evolution illustrates the possibility of preserving institutional continuity while accommodating a changed society. Its achievement lies not in perpetuating colonial privilege but in acquiring a different social meaning. Its history should, therefore, be assessed in the context of what it has become, rather than reduced to the circumstances of its birth.

Its internal electoral system is another important dimension of this evolution. The election of office-bearers by members provides a mechanism of representation and accountability, distinguishing member-based civilian governance from systems dependent entirely on external authority or official appointment.

The transparency of these elections must be judged by the electoral rules, eligibility criteria, fairness of the process and publication of results. Elections alone do not guarantee flawless governance, but neither should an established electoral system be dismissed without examining its actual functioning. Internal democracy does not make a club universally accessible, just as selective membership does not automatically make it unaccountable. These are distinct questions and should be treated as such.

This combination of historical continuity, social adaptation and member-based governance makes Lahore Gymkhana a distinctive institution in Pakistan’s civic landscape. Its survival is not remarkable merely because it has endured; its significance lies in its ability to acquire a place in a society radically different from the one that produced it.

This transformation should neither be romanticised nor dismissed. It deserves recognition alongside an honest examination of the institution’s remaining privileges and obligations.

It is against this background that the current criticism of the club must be judged. Its centrally located land is undeniably valuable, and questions concerning its lease, construction approvals, taxation and financial obligations are legitimate.

No institution should be exempt from the law, and public property must be administered transparently. But accountability is only as credible as the evidence supporting it.

The manner in which a member of the provincial assembly reportedly questioned the club’s chairman raises concerns if inaccurate examples or questionable comparisons are presented as established facts. Parliamentary oversight is a serious responsibility, not political theatre. An elected representative’s authority should be reflected in the accuracy of his information and the fairness of his questions, not merely in the audacity of his confrontation.

The selectivity of this indignation is equally troubling. If public land must be administered equitably, the principle must apply to all institutions, irrespective of their influence or proximity to the state. What comparable scrutiny is directed at garrison clubs, golf courses and other establishments associated with powerful constituencies? What standards govern their leases, concessions and use of public resources?

These questions do not absolve Lahore Gymkhana of accountability; they expose the inconsistency of targeting a civilian institution while comparable arrangements elsewhere may escape equivalent examination. If low rents, unauthorised structures or tax irregularities are objectionable, the same standards must apply across the board. Otherwise, equality before the law becomes a slogan invoked against the accessible while the powerful remain undisturbed.

The value of the club’s land inevitably raises another concern: whether scrutiny is directed towards a genuine public benefit or could create an opportunity to transfer a valuable asset from one privileged constituency to another. The land’s commercial potential makes vigilance necessary, although it does not, by itself, prove that any particular critic is motivated by land-grabbing interests. If the lease is legally defective or financially indefensible, it should be reviewed through lawful procedures. But reclaiming valuable property is not automatically an act of public service.

The authorities must explain what would replace the existing arrangement, who would benefit and whether the city would gain genuinely accessible recreational space or merely another commercially valuable development. Reform must serve the public, not simply change the beneficiaries of privilege.

Lahore Gymkhana should, therefore, be judged on two distinct but related grounds: the legality of its present arrangements and the significance of its institutional transformation. Its colonial origins cannot be condoned, but neither should they become a permanent indictment of an institution whose social context and governance have changed. Its lease must withstand legal and financial scrutiny; its elections should be assessed for transparency; and its evolution after

Partition should be recognised without exaggerating its egalitarian character. Acknowledging institutional progress does not mean granting immunity from accountability.

The real test of accountability is consistency, just as the test of institutional progress is the capacity to change. Pakistan must do more than condemn the exclusions of the Raj: it must subject contemporary privilege to equal scrutiny, regardless of who enjoys it. To single out a civilian club while leaving comparable or greater concentrations of privilege insufficiently examined is not a triumph of democratic accountability but a contradiction of its central principle.

An independent society demonstrates its maturity by judging institutions impartially, recognising genuine adaptation, demanding transparency in the use of public resources and refusing to let political theatre replace evidence.

Lahore Gymkhana’s colonial past should remind us of the injustice of exclusion; its subsequent evolution should remind us that institutions can change. The ultimate standard must be the public interest, not selective indignation or the lure of valuable urban land.

article_html:
The British did not establish clubs in colonial India merely for cricket, golf and other recreations. They formed part of the social architecture of colonial rule, providing civil and military officials with spaces to cultivate networks, consolidate solidarity and preserve racial distinctions.

The exclusion of Indians from establishments reserved for Europeans reflected the belief that political domination conferred social superiority. This history deserves unequivocal condemnation.

Yet condemning an institution’s colonial origins does not automatically invalidate its subsequent existence. Institutions, like societies, can evolve, and their ability to transcend the circumstances of their creation is an important measure of historical adaptation.

Lahore Gymkhana emerged from this world of colonial exclusivity and acquired its present name on March 23, 1906. Its history, however, cannot be frozen at the moment of its inception. Partition in 1947 dismantled the political and social order that had sustained colonial institutions, yet Lahore Gymkhana survived and gradually became part of the civilian life of ‘independent’ Pakistan.

An institution originally designed for a privileged foreign establishment adapted to a different national and social environment, drawing members from professional, business and salaried circles. While it remains selective and cannot be described as wholly egalitarian, its contemporary identity is no longer synonymous with the racial exclusivity of its founders.

It should be borne in mind that salaried individuals are among those whose incomes are taxed at source, and the revenue generated through taxation helps meet government expenditures without relying solely on loans from international institutions. Those crying foul over Gymkhana are privileged individuals who, in many cases, do not bear their fair share of the tax burden.

Anyhow reverting to the transformation deserves recognition, particularly in a country where many inherited institutions changed their personnel after independence without fundamentally altering their hierarchical structures.

Lahore Gymkhana’s evolution illustrates the possibility of preserving institutional continuity while accommodating a changed society. Its achievement lies not in perpetuating colonial privilege but in acquiring a different social meaning. Its history should, therefore, be assessed in the context of what it has become, rather than reduced to the circumstances of its birth.

Its internal electoral system is another important dimension of this evolution. The election of office-bearers by members provides a mechanism of representation and accountability, distinguishing member-based civilian governance from systems dependent entirely on external authority or official appointment.

The transparency of these elections must be judged by the electoral rules, eligibility criteria, fairness of the process and publication of results. Elections alone do not guarantee flawless governance, but neither should an established electoral system be dismissed without examining its actual functioning. Internal democracy does not make a club universally accessible, just as selective membership does not automatically make it unaccountable. These are distinct questions and should be treated as such.

This combination of historical continuity, social adaptation and member-based governance makes Lahore Gymkhana a distinctive institution in Pakistan’s civic landscape. Its survival is not remarkable merely because it has endured; its significance lies in its ability to acquire a place in a society radically different from the one that produced it.

This transformation should neither be romanticised nor dismissed. It deserves recognition alongside an honest examination of the institution’s remaining privileges and obligations.

It is against this background that the current criticism of the club must be judged. Its centrally located land is undeniably valuable, and questions concerning its lease, construction approvals, taxation and financial obligations are legitimate.

No institution should be exempt from the law, and public property must be administered transparently. But accountability is only as credible as the evidence supporting it.

The manner in which a member of the provincial assembly reportedly questioned the club’s chairman raises concerns if inaccurate examples or questionable comparisons are presented as established facts. Parliamentary oversight is a serious responsibility, not political theatre. An elected representative’s authority should be reflected in the accuracy of his information and the fairness of his questions, not merely in the audacity of his confrontation.

The selectivity of this indignation is equally troubling. If public land must be administered equitably, the principle must apply to all institutions, irrespective of their influence or proximity to the state. What comparable scrutiny is directed at garrison clubs, golf courses and other establishments associated with powerful constituencies? What standards govern their leases, concessions and use of public resources?

These questions do not absolve Lahore Gymkhana of accountability; they expose the inconsistency of targeting a civilian institution while comparable arrangements elsewhere may escape equivalent examination. If low rents, unauthorised structures or tax irregularities are objectionable, the same standards must apply across the board. Otherwise, equality before the law becomes a slogan invoked against the accessible while the powerful remain undisturbed.

The value of the club’s land inevitably raises another concern: whether scrutiny is directed towards a genuine public benefit or could create an opportunity to transfer a valuable asset from one privileged constituency to another. The land’s commercial potential makes vigilance necessary, although it does not, by itself, prove that any particular critic is motivated by land-grabbing interests. If the lease is legally defective or financially indefensible, it should be reviewed through lawful procedures. But reclaiming valuable property is not automatically an act of public service.

The authorities must explain what would replace the existing arrangement, who would benefit and whether the city would gain genuinely accessible recreational space or merely another commercially valuable development. Reform must serve the public, not simply change the beneficiaries of privilege.

Lahore Gymkhana should, therefore, be judged on two distinct but related grounds: the legality of its present arrangements and the significance of its institutional transformation. Its colonial origins cannot be condoned, but neither should they become a permanent indictment of an institution whose social context and governance have changed. Its lease must withstand legal and financial scrutiny; its elections should be assessed for transparency; and its evolution after

Partition should be recognised without exaggerating its egalitarian character. Acknowledging institutional progress does not mean granting immunity from accountability.

The real test of accountability is consistency, just as the test of institutional progress is the capacity to change. Pakistan must do more than condemn the exclusions of the Raj: it must subject contemporary privilege to equal scrutiny, regardless of who enjoys it. To single out a civilian club while leaving comparable or greater concentrations of privilege insufficiently examined is not a triumph of democratic accountability but a contradiction of its central principle.

An independent society demonstrates its maturity by judging institutions impartially, recognising genuine adaptation, demanding transparency in the use of public resources and refusing to let political theatre replace evidence.

Lahore Gymkhana’s colonial past should remind us of the injustice of exclusion; its subsequent evolution should remind us that institutions can change. The ultimate standard must be the public interest, not selective indignation or the lure of valuable urban land.

headline: In Spectrum: Gymkhana: colonial origins and politics of selective outrage
description: Institutions, like societies, can evolve, and their ability to transcend the circumstances of their creation is an important measure of historical adaptation.
author: Tahir Kamran
article_text:
The British did not establish clubs in colonial India merely for cricket, golf and other recreations. They formed part of the social architecture of colonial rule, providing civil and military officials with spaces to cultivate networks, consolidate solidarity and preserve racial distinctions.

The exclusion of Indians from establishments reserved for Europeans reflected the belief that political domination conferred social superiority. This history deserves unequivocal condemnation.

Yet condemning an institution’s colonial origins does not automatically invalidate its subsequent existence. Institutions, like societies, can evolve, and their ability to transcend the circumstances of their creation is an important measure of historical adaptation.

Lahore Gymkhana emerged from this world of colonial exclusivity and acquired its present name on March 23, 1906. Its history, however, cannot be frozen at the moment of its inception. Partition in 1947 dismantled the political and social order that had sustained colonial institutions, yet Lahore Gymkhana survived and gradually became part of the civilian life of ‘independent’ Pakistan.

An institution originally designed for a privileged foreign establishment adapted to a different national and social environment, drawing members from professional, business and salaried circles. While it remains selective and cannot be described as wholly egalitarian, its contemporary identity is no longer synonymous with the racial exclusivity of its founders.

It should be borne in mind that salaried individuals are among those whose incomes are taxed at source, and the revenue generated through taxation helps meet government expenditures without relying solely on loans from international institutions. Those crying foul over Gymkhana are privileged individuals who, in many cases, do not bear their fair share of the tax burden.

Anyhow reverting to the transformation deserves recognition, particularly in a country where many inherited institutions changed their personnel after independence without fundamentally altering their hierarchical structures.

Lahore Gymkhana’s evolution illustrates the possibility of preserving institutional continuity while accommodating a changed society. Its achievement lies not in perpetuating colonial privilege but in acquiring a different social meaning. Its history should, therefore, be assessed in the context of what it has become, rather than reduced to the circumstances of its birth.

Its internal electoral system is another important dimension of this evolution. The election of office-bearers by members provides a mechanism of representation and accountability, distinguishing member-based civilian governance from systems dependent entirely on external authority or official appointment.

The transparency of these elections must be judged by the electoral rules, eligibility criteria, fairness of the process and publication of results. Elections alone do not guarantee flawless governance, but neither should an established electoral system be dismissed without examining its actual functioning. Internal democracy does not make a club universally accessible, just as selective membership does not automatically make it unaccountable. These are distinct questions and should be treated as such.

This combination of historical continuity, social adaptation and member-based governance makes Lahore Gymkhana a distinctive institution in Pakistan’s civic landscape. Its survival is not remarkable merely because it has endured; its significance lies in its ability to acquire a place in a society radically different from the one that produced it.

This transformation should neither be romanticised nor dismissed. It deserves recognition alongside an honest examination of the institution’s remaining privileges and obligations.

It is against this background that the current criticism of the club must be judged. Its centrally located land is undeniably valuable, and questions concerning its lease, construction approvals, taxation and financial obligations are legitimate.

No institution should be exempt from the law, and public property must be administered transparently. But accountability is only as credible as the evidence supporting it.

The manner in which a member of the provincial assembly reportedly questioned the club’s chairman raises concerns if inaccurate examples or questionable comparisons are presented as established facts. Parliamentary oversight is a serious responsibility, not political theatre. An elected representative’s authority should be reflected in the accuracy of his information and the fairness of his questions, not merely in the audacity of his confrontation.

The selectivity of this indignation is equally troubling. If public land must be administered equitably, the principle must apply to all institutions, irrespective of their influence or proximity to the state. What comparable scrutiny is directed at garrison clubs, golf courses and other establishments associated with powerful constituencies? What standards govern their leases, concessions and use of public resources?

These questions do not absolve Lahore Gymkhana of accountability; they expose the inconsistency of targeting a civilian institution while comparable arrangements elsewhere may escape equivalent examination. If low rents, unauthorised structures or tax irregularities are objectionable, the same standards must apply across the board. Otherwise, equality before the law becomes a slogan invoked against the accessible while the powerful remain undisturbed.

The value of the club’s land inevitably raises another concern: whether scrutiny is directed towards a genuine public benefit or could create an opportunity to transfer a valuable asset from one privileged constituency to another. The land’s commercial potential makes vigilance necessary, although it does not, by itself, prove that any particular critic is motivated by land-grabbing interests. They formed part of the social architecture of colonial rule, providing civil and military officials with spaces to cultivate networks, consolidate solidarity and preserve racial distinctions.
The exclusion of Indians from establishments reserved for Europeans reflected the belief that political domination conferred social superiority. This history deserves unequivocal condemnation.

Yet condemning an institution’s colonial origins does not automatically invalidate its subsequent existence. Institutions, like societies, can evolve, and their ability to transcend the circumstances of their creation is an important measure of historical adaptation.

Lahore Gymkhana emerged from this world of colonial exclusivity and acquired its present name on March 23, 1906. Its history, however, cannot be frozen at the moment of its inception. Partition in 1947 dismantled the political and social order that had sustained colonial institutions, yet Lahore Gymkhana survived and gradually became part of the civilian life of ‘independent’ Pakistan.

An institution originally designed for a privileged foreign establishment adapted to a different national and social environment, drawing members from professional, business and salaried circles. While it remains selective and cannot be described as wholly egalitarian, its contemporary identity is no longer synonymous with the racial exclusivity of its founders.

It should be borne in mind that salaried individuals are among those whose incomes are taxed at source, and the revenue generated through taxation helps meet government expenditures without relying solely on loans from international institutions. Those crying foul over Gymkhana are privileged individuals who, in many cases, do not bear their fair share of the tax burden.

Anyhow reverting to the transformation deserves recognition, particularly in a country where many inherited institutions changed their personnel after independence without fundamentally altering their hierarchical structures.

Lahore Gymkhana’s evolution illustrates the possibility of preserving institutional continuity while accommodating a changed society. Its achievement lies not in perpetuating colonial privilege but in acquiring a different social meaning. Its history should, therefore, be assessed in the context of what it has become, rather than reduced to the circumstances of its birth.

Its internal electoral system is another important dimension of this evolution. The election of office-bearers by members provides a mechanism of representation and accountability, distinguishing member-based civilian governance from systems dependent entirely on external authority or official appointment.

The transparency of these elections must be judged by the electoral rules, eligibility criteria, fairness of the process and publication of results. Elections alone do not guarantee flawless governance, but neither should an established electoral system be dismissed without examining its actual functioning. Internal democracy does not make a club universally accessible, just as selective membership does not automatically make it unaccountable. These are distinct questions and should be treated as such.

This combination of historical continuity, social adaptation and member-based governance makes Lahore Gymkhana a distinctive institution in Pakistan’s civic landscape. Its survival is not remarkable merely because it has endured; its significance lies in its ability to acquire a place in a society radically different from the one that produced it.
This transformation should neither be romanticised nor dismissed. It deserves recognition alongside an honest examination of the institution’s remaining privileges and obligations.

It is against this background that the current criticism of the club must be judged. Its centrally located land is undeniably valuable, and questions concerning its lease, construction approvals, taxation and financial obligations are legitimate.
No institution should be exempt from the law, and public property must be administered transparently. But accountability is only as credible as the evidence supporting it.

The manner in which a member of the provincial assembly reportedly questioned the club’s chairman raises concerns if inaccurate examples or questionable comparisons are presented as established facts. Parliamentary oversight is a serious responsibility, not political theatre. An elected representative’s authority should be reflected in the accuracy of his information and the fairness of his questions, not merely in the audacity of his confrontation.

The selectivity of this indignation is equally troubling. If public land must be administered equitably, the principle must apply to all institutions, irrespective of their influence or proximity to the state. What comparable scrutiny is directed at garrison clubs, golf courses and other establishments associated with powerful constituencies? What standards govern their leases, concessions and use of public resources?

These questions do not absolve Lahore Gymkhana of accountability; they expose the inconsistency of targeting a civilian institution while comparable arrangements elsewhere may escape equivalent examination. If low rents, unauthorised structures or tax irregularities are objectionable, the same standards must apply across the board. Otherwise, equality before the law becomes a slogan invoked against the accessible while the powerful remain undisturbed.

The value of the club’s land inevitably raises another concern: whether scrutiny is directed towards a genuine public benefit or could create an opportunity to transfer a valuable asset from one privileged constituency to another. The land’s commercial potential makes vigilance necessary, although it does not, by itself, prove that any particular critic is motivated by land-grabbing interests. If the lease is legally defective or financially indefensible, it should be reviewed through lawful procedures. But reclaiming valuable property is not automatically an act of public service.

The authorities must explain what would replace the existing arrangement, who would benefit and whether the city would gain genuinely accessible recreational space or merely another commercially valuable development. Reform must serve the public, not simply change the beneficiaries of privilege.

Lahore Gymkhana should, therefore, be judged on two distinct but related grounds: the legality of its present arrangements and the significance of its institutional transformation. Its colonial origins cannot be condoned, but neither should they become a permanent indictment of an institution whose social context and governance have changed. Its lease must withstand legal and financial scrutiny; its elections should be assessed for transparency; and its evolution after
Partition should be recognised without exaggerating its egalitarian character. Acknowledging institutional progress does not mean granting immunity from accountability.

The real test of accountability is consistency, just as the test of institutional progress is the capacity to change. Pakistan must do more than condemn the exclusions of the Raj: it must subject contemporary privilege to equal scrutiny, regardless of who enjoys it. To single out a civilian club while leaving comparable or greater concentrations of privilege insufficiently examined is not a triumph of democratic accountability but a contradiction of its central principle.

An independent society demonstrates its maturity by judging institutions impartially, recognising genuine adaptation, demanding transparency in the use of public resources and refusing to let political theatre replace evidence.

Lahore Gymkhana’s colonial past should remind us of the injustice of exclusion; its subsequent evolution should remind us that institutions can change. The ultimate standard must be the public interest, not selective indignation or the lure of valuable urban land.
Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: World Bank okays $150m plan to boost property tax collection in Karachi
description: Programme will support the Sindh government in improving urban immovable property tax collection and strengthening municipal service delivery capacity in selected local councils of Sindh.
author: Amin Ahmed
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: The World Bank has approved a $150 million programme to help the Sindh government improve urban property tax collection and strengthen municipal service delivery in 25 towns of Karachi.

The Sindh Property Revenues Enhancement Programme (Sindh PREP) approved by the World Bank board of executive directors, will benefit Karachi’s 25 local councils. Its primary beneficiaries are the 3.58 million people living in these councils, where service delivery investments will be financed, the World Bank resident mission in Islamabad announced on Saturday.

The programme will support the Sindh government in improving urban immovable property tax (UIPT) collection and strengthening municipal service delivery capacity in selected local councils of Sindh.

“Cities that can raise their own revenues can plan and invest for the long term,” said Bolormaa Amgaabazar, World Bank Country Director for Pakistan. “Today, Sindh’s local councils depend on provincial transfers for more than 95 per cent of their revenues. By helping Karachi collect the property taxes from its residents and businesses, and by reinvesting most of that revenue in local services, this programme will give Sindh’s cities the means to finance the infrastructure they need.”

About 70 percent of collected UIPT revenues will be reinvested directly into municipal infrastructure and services in participating local councils.

“Karachi has significant untapped potential to generate revenues from its property base and use those resources to fund the infrastructure its residents and businesses need. This programme will help Sindh strengthen fiscal sustainability enabling cities to plan, invest, and deliver services from their own resources effectively,” said Davison Muchadenyika, senior urban development specialist at the World Bank.

headline: Kasur woman suffers burns in acid attack by brother-in-law
description: The victim alleged the suspect had been harassing her for some time and forcing her to have a physical relation with him.
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
KASUR: A woman was seriously injured after her brother-in-law allegedly threw acid on her in the Purani Mandi Area in the limits of Pattoki City police station on Saturday.

According to the police, Shahbaz allegedly threw acid on his sister-in-law, leaving her in a seriously injured condition with burns on her face and other parts of the body. Police shifted the injured to the THQ Hospital for medical treatment.

The victim, Fatima Bibi (20), in her initial statement to the police alleged the suspect had been harassing her for some time and forcing her to have a physical relation with him. She claimed that on her refusal, he threw acid on her to teach her a lesson.

Police were looking into the matter and no arrest had been made so far in the case.

ATTACK: Two brothers were injured on Saturday in an alleged armed attack by their rivals over pursuing a case at a local court near Sheikhum village on the Kasur-Kot Radha Kishan Road.

According to police, Abu Bakar (20) and his brother Abu Hanan (18) were on their way to the district courts in connection with an ongoing litigation. When the brothers, riding a bike, reached near Sheikhum village, their rivals opened indiscriminate firing on them.

As a result, both suffered injuries and were rushed to the DHQ Hospital, where their condition was said to be critical.

Police were looking into the matter.

ELECTROCUTION: A 12-year-old boy was electrocuted after live wires fell on him at Ratti Pindi village in the limits of Kot Radha Kishan police station.

Police said low-lying wires fell down on the boy after entangling with a tractor trolley that was passing through the street.

The boy died instantly and Rescue 1122 shifted the body to the Kot Radha Kishan THQ Hospital.

Police handed over the body to the bereaved family after legal formalities.

headline: Two dead as car, bike fall into canal after collision in Multan
description: Four people, including two women, were riding the motorcycle when it collided with the car.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
LAHORE: A man and a woman were killed while another woman and a two-year-old girl were injured when a car collided with a motorcycle and both vehicles fell into a canal near Muhammad Nawaz Sharif University of Agriculture, Multan on Saturday.

Four people, including two women, were riding the motorcycle when it collided with the car. The deceased were identified as Bilal, 27, and his wife, Sobia, 24. Both suffered head injuries and died at the scene. The injured were identified as Saadia, 19, and two-year-old Hoor, daughter of Bilal. They sustained serious injuries and were shifted to the Nishtar Hospital.

Rescue teams launched an operation to retrieve the vehicles from the canal and conduct a search. The car driver fled the scene after the accident.

Separately, Multan Rescue 1122 responded to 469 emergencies across the district during the last 24 hours, rescuing 472 people, according to its daily report issued on Saturday.

Of the reported emergencies, 437 occurred in Multan city, 19 in Shujabad and 13 in Jalalpur Pirwala.

The district recorded 105 road accidents and 272 medical emergencies during the period. In addition, four fire incidents, 10 crime-related incidents and 12 fall-related emergencies were reported.

headline: KP govt to shortly execute Saudi-funded water supply project
description: The mega water supply project aimed to provide a reliable, safe and sustainable supply of drinking water to residents.
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
MANSEHRA: The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government, with financial assistance from the Saudi Fund for Development, is set to execute a Rs19 billion gravity-flow water supply scheme to meet the longstanding demand for potable water in the city and its suburbs here.

“The federal government has signed an agreement with the Saudi Fund for Development to finance a substantial portion of the Rs19 billion gravity-flow water supply scheme. Work on the project is expected to commence shortly,” Project Director Abid Shah told reporters on Saturday.

He said it was one of the biggest potable water supply schemes ever launched by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government with financial assistance from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

“The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Public Health Engineering Department is making rapid progress on the Rs19 billion gravity-flow water supply scheme, which is being undertaken with financial assistance from the Saudi Fund for Development,” Mr Shah said.

He said the mega water supply project aimed to provide a reliable, safe and sustainable supply of drinking water to residents.

“We will lay a 65-kilometre-long pipeline from its water source at Neeli Nadi in the environmentally sensitive Sharan area, situated between Kaghan and Manoor valleys,” Mr Shah said.

He said Deputy Commissioner Yasir Ali Khan was also extending full support to ensure the timely execution of the mega project and the provision of potable water to the residents of the city and its suburbs.

“We will construct a modern water treatment plant, storage reservoirs and an improved distribution network relying on gravity rather than conventional pumping systems. This will reduce energy costs and ensure long-term operational sustainability,” Mr Shah said.

He said the project management unit was actively coordinating with the Saudi Fund for Development, the federal Economic Affairs Division and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Planning and Development Department to expedite the necessary processes and ensure smooth and timely implementation.

headline: Disciplinary proceedings against Karachi's Valika hospital employees over HIV outbreak slow, regrets ombudsman
description: Says he had finalised hearing of complaints about 170 HIV cases at the facility.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Correspondent
article_text:
HYDERABAD: Sindh Ombuds­man Dr Mohammad Sohail Rajput, who is a former chief secretary of Sindh, has expressed his disappointment over the slow pace of disciplinary proceedings against 64 employees of the Kulsoom Bai Valika Hospital over an HIV outbreak there.

He was speaking to journalists at the local press club on Saturday evening. President Junaid Khanzada and Secretary Ashok Sharma of the club welcomed him and his team.

The ombudsman said that his office had finalised the criminal proceedings against these employees of the hospital [run under the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution], “but it is unfortunate to see the disciplinary proceeding against them at a slow pace”.

He recalled that 170 HIV cases had been reported from the hospital after which he heard the complaints. Some infected children were socially isolated, rather expelled from the school, but his office ensured that they continue their education. He said these children were infected only because of reuse of syringes at the hospital. Children of one family were all infected and tested positive for HIV, he said.

Says he had finalised hearing of complaints about 170 HIV cases at the facility

The ombudsman said that people need to trust the ombudsman office, which has been addressing their grievances regarding various government departments and agencies. “This is visible from the large number of complaints being disposed of by this office annually,” he said, and stressed that legal reforms could ensure implementation of all its decisions.

He noted that most complaints from rural Sindh pertained to the education and health sectors which he was focusing on considering the fact that loss of education and health were always irreversible. The civic and infrastructure issues could be resolved belatedly, he believed.

Mr Rajput said that there were around 8,000 complaints that used to be handled by this office annually until he took the charge of the ombudsman’s office. “Now the average annual number is around 25,000 i.e. three times higher,” he pointed out. He said 90pc of these complaints are decided within a 90-day timeline.

He said that the ratio of complaint submission had substantially increased because of some initiatives taken after 2024. Still this increase is on a lower side given Sindh’s population i.e. 55 million, he viewed.

Explaining the initiatives, the ombudsman said his office engaged 10 brand ambassadors, from each of Sindh’s universities, for the projection of the office’s working through digital means. He said that now complainants had been given more visibility as they could check the status of their complaints online and remain aware of the relevant proceedings.

Generally, he said, people felt that the ombudsman’s office is after all a government entity thus its intervention would not be that much effective.

Mr Rajput said that in the case of Karachi, complainants come up with grievances against the police department, Sindh Building Control Authority and Karachi Water & Sewerage Board, but the positive aspect which may be noted is the case of rural Sindh, where people appeared to be more concerned about the education sector.

“Teachers are either not available or they lack teaching skills,” he said, and added that if a primary school student loses education in the first five years, the loss would always be irreversible.

The ombudsman said he had personally visited schools in Kharo Chhan and Keti Bunder (Thatta-Sujawal region) where children wouldn’t be able to compete with their counterparts from other areas. He said many of those he spoke to only expressed a desire to seek a government or clerical job. “How can these children achieve something big in their life when they don’t aim for something big in life?” he wondered. To him, he said, it was a disparity.

He said in Sindhri, Mirpurkhas district he was told that teachers were not available and this was in spite of the fact that merit-based appointments were made through the Sukkur IBA. He said that it was a matter of administrative slackness, and not a lack of resources. He said that he would be bringing the situation to the notice of the Sindh chief minister.

Turning to the Liaquat University Hospital (LUH), Hyderabad, the ombudsman said it needed expansion and administrative efficiency to ensure better healthcare services. This hospital, developed by the Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences, is a good addition at Jamshoro, he said. “The LUMHS vice chancellor had told me that it would become a 200-bed hospital with provision of more services of specialties,” said Ombudsman Rajput.

The ombudsman said that his office had finalised the criminal proceedings against these employees of the hospital [run under the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution], “but it is unfortunate to see the disciplinary proceeding against them at a slow pace”.

He recalled that 170 HIV cases had been reported from the hospital after which he heard the complaints. Some infected children were socially isolated, rather expelled from the school, but his office ensured that they continue their education. He said these children were infected only because of reuse of syringes at the hospital. Children of one family were all infected and tested positive for HIV, he said.

Says he had finalised hearing of complaints about 170 HIV cases at the facility

The ombudsman said that people need to trust the ombudsman office, which has been addressing their grievances regarding various government departments and agencies. “This is visible from the large number of complaints being disposed of by this office annually,” he said, and stressed that legal reforms could ensure implementation of all its decisions.

He noted that most complaints from rural Sindh pertained to the education and health sectors which he was focusing on considering the fact that loss of education and health were always irreversible. The civic and infrastructure issues could be resolved belatedly, he believed.

Mr Rajput said that there were around 8,000 complaints that used to be handled by this office annually until he took the charge of the ombudsman’s office. “Now the average annual number is around 25,000 i.e. three times higher,” he pointed out. He said 90pc of these complaints are decided within a 90-day timeline.

He said that the ratio of complaint submission had substantially increased because of some initiatives taken after 2024. Still this increase is on a lower side given Sindh’s population i.e. 55 million, he viewed.

Explaining the initiatives, the ombudsman said his office engaged 10 brand ambassadors, from each of Sindh’s universities, for the projection of the office’s working through digital means. He said that now complainants had been given more visibility as they could check the status of their complaints online and remain aware of the relevant proceedings.

Generally, he said, people felt that the ombudsman’s office is after all a government entity thus its intervention would not be that much effective.

Mr Rajput said that in the case of Karachi, complainants come up with grievances against the police department, Sindh Building Control Authority and Karachi Water & Sewerage Board, but the positive aspect which may be noted is the case of rural Sindh, where people appeared to be more concerned about the education sector.

“Teachers are either not available or they lack teaching skills,” he said, and added that if a primary school student loses education in the first five years, the loss would always be irreversible.

The ombudsman said he had personally visited schools in Kharo Chhan and Keti Bunder (Thatta-Sujawal region) where children wouldn’t be able to compete with their counterparts from other areas. He said many of those he spoke to only expressed a desire to seek a government or clerical job. “How can these children achieve something big in their life when they don’t aim for something big in life?” he wondered. To him, he said, it was a disparity.

He said in Sindhri, Mirpurkhas district he was told that teachers were not available and this was in spite of the fact that merit-based appointments were made through the Sukkur IBA. He said that it was a matter of administrative slackness, and not a lack of resources. He said that he would be bringing the situation to the notice of the Sindh chief minister.

Turning to the Liaquat University Hospital (LUH), Hyderabad, the ombudsman said it needed expansion and administrative efficiency to ensure better healthcare services. This hospital, developed by the Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences, is a good addition at Jamshoro, he said. “The LUMHS vice chancellor had told me that it would become a 200-bed hospital with provision of more services of specialties,” said Ombudsman Rajput.

headline: Mob torches trailer after pregnant woman’s death in Karachi's Liaquatabad
description: Traffic police officer says the woman and her husband were travelling on a motorbike when the trailer hit them.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
KARACHI: Enraged people set a trailer on fire after it ran over and killed a pregnant woman and injured her husband in a road accident in Liaquatabad, police said on Saturday.

A traffic police officer said that the couple was travelling on a motorbike when the trailer hit them as they descended from the Liaquatabad flyover and approached the Sindh Government Hospital Liaquatabad on S M Taufiq Road.

Both sustained critical injuries and were taken to the Abbasi Shaheed Hospital (ASH), where Faiza, 45, was pronounced dead. Her husband, Fahim, 55, was admitted for treatment.

Officials said the deceased woman, who was said to be full-term pregnant, was returning after a medical check-up.

The driver fled the scene and abandoned the heavy vehicle, which was subsequently set on fire by an angry mob.

The police said reckless driving was believed to be the probable cause of the accident.

In a separate incident, a young motorcyclist was killed on the Superhighway, police and rescue services officials said.

They said the man, later identified as Asif, was riding his motorbike when a trailer hit him near Jamali Bridge.

He was taken to the ASH, where he was pronounced dead.

SITE-Superhighway Industrial Area SHO Mohammad Nawaz said the driver fled the scene, while police had seized the heavy vehicle.

A Rescue-1122 spokesperson said that the mob did not allow firemen and law enforcers to extinguish the blaze.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: Woman dies by suicide after ‘strangling’ minor daughter in Bajaur
description: A police official said the bodies were taken to the District Headquarters Hospital in Khar for postmortem.
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
BAJAUR: A woman allegedly committed suicide after ‘strangling’ her minor daughter to death in War Mamond tehsil of Bajaur district on Saturday, police and residents said.

They said that the incident had occurred in the hilly Wara Kharkai area in the limits of War Mamond police station.

They said the woman, whose identity could not be ascertained, first allegedly strangled her minor daughter to death and then hanged herself inside her home for unknown reasons.

A police official told Dawn that a team rushed to the spot after receiving information about the incident and the bodies were taken to the District Headquarters Hospital in Khar for postmortem.

The bodies were handed over to relatives for burial after the postmortem.

Mansoor Khan, a spokesperson for the district police, told reporters that an investigation had been launched to ascertain the causes behind the incident.

Meanwhile, an person was killed after unidentified gunmen opened fire on him in Mina Bazaar of Lowi Mamond tehsil on Friday night.

Police and residents said Malik Tamreez Khan, 57, was on his way to home when the assailants targeted him, leaving him wounded.

He was taken to the District Headquarters Hospital in Khar where he succumbed to injuries.

Police have launched an investigation to ascertain the motive behind the killing and bring the perpetrators to justice.

headline: 12 dilapidated classrooms of Charsadda school sealed
description: Inspection was conducted on the directives of the chief secretary.
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
CHARSADDA: The district education officer (DEO) on Saturday ordered the sealing of 12 classrooms and the principal’s office at Government Shaheed Tariq Sentinel Model High School in Turangzai here, and the shifting of students to safer rooms due to the deteriorating condition of the building.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Secretary Dr Mohammad Fakhre Alam Irfan had taken notice of the dilapidated condition of the school building after reports and photographs highlighting the plight of students went viral on social media.

DEO Fazal Wahid visited the school accompanied by deputy DEO Zubair Khalil, DEO planning and development Shiraz Hussain and other officials.

The school principal, Mohammad Ayaz Khan, briefed the officials on the deteriorating condition of the building, difficulties faced by students and the impact on academic activities.

Talking to journalists, Mr Wahid said the inspection had been conducted on the directives of the chief secretary and that the safety of students was the department’s top priority.

He directed the school administration to ensure that academic activities continued without interruption and that all available facilities were utilised to provide students with a safe learning environment.

“The lives of children are our foremost priority, and no compromise will be made on their safety,” he said, adding that steps would be taken soon for the reconstruction of the dilapidated building.

MAN GETS LIFE: A court in Tangi has sentenced a man to life imprisonment after convicting him of the murder of a medic, Dr Faisal Sardar, who was killed on June 6, 2018.

Additional Sessions Judge Islamuddin Khan also awarded the convict, Khan Badshah, 10 years’ imprisonment under Section 324 of the Pakistan Penal Code (attempted murder) and three years’ imprisonment, along with a fine of Rs500,000, in the case involving the recovery of a Kalashnikov.

Advocate Malik Fida Hussain Khalil represented the complainant’s side, while Yousaf Shah Mohmand appeared on behalf of the convict.

The verdict marks a significant development in the eight-year-old murder case, while the investigation conducted by Sub-Inspector Muzaffar Khan played an important role in bringing the case to its conclusion.

headline: Woman shifted to LGH through air ambulance
description: The woman accidentally fell down from the roof of her house and was seriously injured.
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
MIANWALI: A seriously injured woman was shifted from Mianwali to Lahore through an air ambulance.

The woman accidentally fell down from the roof of her house and was seriously injured. She was admitted to the DHQ Hospital (Mianwali) but did not recover.

Local doctors suggested her shifting to Lahore for better treatment there. Rescue 1122 shifted her from the DHQ Hospital to the General Hospital, Lahore, through air ambulance.

headline: Official records ‘stolen’ from Bannu TMA office
description: Administration said that the drawers and cupboards of the branch were found unlocked when the office reopened last Monday.
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
BANNU: The theft of official records from the Tehsil Municipal Administration (TMA), Bannu, has come to light, with important registers and files reportedly missing from the Tehsil Officer Regulation (TOR) branch.

In a complaint submitted to the city police station, the administration said that the drawers and cupboards of the branch were found unlocked when the office reopened last Monday.

According to an internal report by a senior assistant of the TOR branch, Rahatullah Shah said, the missing records included the Mazari Mandi records, D&C register, goods warehouse (Mal Mandi) records, entry fee records, and all challan books and files related to Fazal Qadir Shaheed Park.

The report further disclosed that the office keys remained in the possession of an employee last Saturday and Sunday.

TMA Bannu Tehsil Municipal Officer Fakhrul Islam requested the police to register a first information report and launch an investigation to recover the missing official records.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: IRGC commander says Iranian forces ‘ready for any enemy scenario’
description: Brigadier-General Yadollah Javani, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ deputy for political affairs, says Iranian...
article_text:
Brigadier-General Yadollah Javani, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ deputy for political affairs, says Iranian forces are operating on the assumption that the US or Israel could strike at any moment, Al Jazeera reports.

He has told the semi-official Fars news agency that the military is “fully prepared for any scenario the enemy may devise”, and that Iran will not be caught off guard and will respond as necessary.

Javani says Iran’s military capabilities now allow it to confront the enemy not only defensively but also through preemptive and offensive operations.

He said Iran can inflict heavy, devastating strikes on US warships and warned that any region that enemy forces try to enter — whether by air assault or across a border — would become a “killing ground” for them.

article_text:
Two air raids hit oil facility in Yemen’s Hodeidah, media report says, according to Al Jazeera.

The Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reports that the Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebel group in Yemen has conducted two raids on an oil facility in Bajil district in western Hodeidah governorate.

It says at least three civilians were wounded.

There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition.

headline: Binance to resume withdrawals after covering bulk of stolen $6.3bn
description: FBI says North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor responsible for the crypto theft.
author: Reuters
article_text:
Binance, the worlds biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said it would resume withdrawals on Sunday after covering 95 per cent of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform in the world’s largest digital heist, which the FBI has tied to North Korea.

The exchange, founded in China, said the first phase of withdrawals would start between 0600 and 0900 GMT and cover 15 crypto assets including bitcoin, ether, XRP, dogecoin and others.

Binance said on Sunday it had covered $6bn of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5pc of stolen tokens consist of assets that are less liquid and may take longer to source in the required amounts, according to the exchange.

FBI ties attack to North Korea unit

The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts.

Last year, attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.

The FBI said on Saturday the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack.

Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.

Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected “further laundering” of the assets through the use of related technology.

Analysts had blamed North Korea and said the Binance theft could be the largest financial heist of all time.

The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.

US President Donald Trump, however, said on Saturday that the US was still not certain if North Korea was involved.

“We don’t know if it’s North Korea but if it is, we’ll talk to North Korea about it,” Trump told reporters on Saturday in comments posted by a White House handle on X.

Binance vows to bear financial costs

Binance has been working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3bn located as of Friday, it said.

The exchange has repeatedly said it would bear the financial impact of the funds stolen in the hack. It has set aside around $6.34bn of company funds internally to cover the losses.

The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance’s $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users( Safu), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X.

Co-CEO Yi He said on Saturday that 50pc of its Safu funds would be used, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about $1 bn.

Richard Teng, the other co-CEO, has said that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.

Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after the hack.

Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

article_html:
Binance, the worlds biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said it would resume withdrawals on Sunday after covering 95 per cent of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform in the world’s largest digital heist, which the FBI has tied to North Korea.

The exchange, founded in China, said the first phase of withdrawals would start between 0600 and 0900 GMT and cover 15 crypto assets including bitcoin, ether, XRP, dogecoin and others.

Binance said on Sunday it had covered $6bn of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5pc of stolen tokens consist of assets that are less liquid and may take longer to source in the required amounts, according to the exchange.

FBI ties attack to North Korea unit

The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts.

Last year, attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.

The FBI said on Saturday the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack.

Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.

Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected “further laundering” of the assets through the use of related technology.

Analysts had blamed North Korea and said the Binance theft could be the largest financial heist of all time.

The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.

US President Donald Trump, however, said on Saturday that the US was still not certain if North Korea was involved.

“We don’t know if it’s North Korea but if it is, we’ll talk to North Korea about it,” Trump told reporters on Saturday in comments posted by a White House handle on X.

Binance vows to bear financial costs

Binance has been working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3bn located as of Friday, it said.

The exchange has repeatedly said it would bear the financial impact of the funds stolen in the hack. It has set aside around $6.34bn of company funds internally to cover the losses.

The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance’s $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users( Safu), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X.

Co-CEO Yi He said on Saturday that 50pc of its Safu funds would be used, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about $1 bn.

Richard Teng, the other co-CEO, has said that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.

Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after the hack.

Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

headline: North Korea tests cluster-bomb warheads: KCNA
description: Officials say the test confirmed the weapon “is capable of turning into ashes a target area of 12 to 13 hectares with its highest-density power”.
author: AFP
article_text:
North Korea test-fired cluster-bomb warheads, its state media reported on Sunday, the latest in a slew of weapons drills aimed at training its military units on using them.

The test, conducted on Saturday, came after the nuclear-armed North recently trialled a range of weaponry including attack drones, a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.

It also came against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.

The North has denied responsibility and vowed to further fortify its border areas and resume its loudspeaker campaign.

Saturday’s test was conducted to “assess adaptation to combat and power of a cluster-bomb warhead to be tipped on tactical ballistic missiles”, the official Korean Central News Agency reported on Sunday.

Officials said it confirmed the weapon “is capable of turning into ashes a target area of 12 to 13 hectares with its highest-density power”.

“Within this year we will enable units to select and use all those types according to operational aims and specific features of targets,” said the general director of the North’s Missile Administration.

Photos released by KCNA showed a projectile firing from a mobile launcher, with an orange exhaust plume. Another image showed multiple cluster-bomb impacts on an island target.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un was not present on Saturday, although he had overseen a test-launch of cluster-bomb warheads mounted on a ballistic missile in April, accompanied by his daughter Ju Ae.

“In the event of a new war, its scope will not be confined to West Asia,” he added.
