headline: Broken record: constitution, commander, curfew.
description: As the pages of Dawn in the weeks after independence show, the country’s founders wanted the country to be run as per the rule of law, not anyone’s personal whims.
author: Qasim A. Moini
article_text:
The issues of Dawn from Sept 1-7, 1947 chronicled the adoption of the Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order as the country’s working constitution, while the nation’s first commander-in-chief issued a stern call for order to control communal violence. Moreover, the city of Karachi — which has been no stranger to violence over the decades — saw its first curfew as the capital of Pakistan.

Constitutional underpinnings

Constitutional tinkering by powerful, often unelected forces has been a sad constant throughout Pakistan’s history. But as the pages of Dawn in the weeks after independence showed, the country’s founders wanted the country to be run as per the rule of law, not anyone’s personal whims.

The lede story in the Sept 3, 1947, edition noted that “the Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order, an adaptation of the Government of India Act, 1935” would serve as the dominion’s temporary constitution. Of course Pakistan would not have its first proper constitution until 1956, largely owing to the political tumult of the early years.

The Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order sought to do away with the vestiges of empire, and give a fresh direction to the country. The news story noted that the law “does away with expressions like “in his discretion” and “exercising his individual judgment”, found in the India Act.”

“Another important feature is absence of any reference to the King anywhere. All appointments including those of the provincial Governors and High Court Judges, will be made by the Governor-General.” Moreover, the oath of office would be sworn to the “Pakistan Constitution and not to the Crown.”

From these reports, it is clear that the original plan envisaged a farewell to British kings and queens, and constitutional supremacy. Little did the founders of Pakistan know that in the decades to come, many uncrowned local ‘kings’ would trample the Constitution, and attempt to dictate terms to the hapless populace of this country.

The general’s call

Two weeks after independence, the fires of communal violence continued to burn, despite repeated appeals by none other than the Quaid for calm. The situation was such that the Pakistan’s army’s first commander-in-chief — Gen Sir Frank Masservy, a British officer — issued a plea for peace in the Sept 1 issue.

In a special order to all ranks of the army, the C-in-C noted that “our main duty … in conjunction with the civil authorities and the police is the difficult and unpleasant one of maintaining law and order and of stopping bloodshed and murder, looting and arson. …”

The general told his men that there would be zero tolerance for law breakers and other undesirables that were stirring up trouble. “The first type of goondas are goondas, dakus and badmashes. These are enemies of the State and must be hunted out and captured or shot. …

“The second type are ignorant citizens and countrymen who get carried away by feelings of revenge … and vent their wrath on the opposite community with the utmost savagery. These two are also enemies of the State tough they may not realise it. …”

These were certainly stern words from the general. But perhaps desperate times called for desperate measures.

Petrol rationing

Pakistanis, as well as consumers around the world, are paying high prices for gasoline and other fuel products derived from hydrocarbons due to the situation created by the US/Israeli war on Iran. There is also the fear of shortages should things get ugly again in the Gulf; in other countries, there have been riots related to fuel shortages, though Pakistan has thankfully been spared such violence till now.

In Sept 1947, however, the state had to resort to rationing of gasoline as communal disturbances in India had disrupted supplies of coal, putting extra pressure on the available fuel stocks. As a news report highlighted in the Sept 2 issue, “the Government of Pakistan has decided to reduce the present ratio of motor spirit from two gallons per unit to one gallon per unit, in Western Pakistan. This step is taken in order to conserve all the available fuel supply. …”

The decision was made “owing to the disturbances in East Punjab” which had caused interruption in the regular supply of coal to Pakistan from India.

Karachi under curfew

Younger readers, particularly those born in the mid-1990s and thereafter, would not have any memory of a curfew clamped on Karachi. But older readers will recall with dread the days and nights the metropolis used to be placed under curfew during the 1980s and early 1990s due to the rampant political and ethnic violence of those bad old days.

In effect it was an order from the state to shelter in place; unless you had a curfew pass, the law-enforcement agencies — often including the military — would not let you move about freely to quell spasms of violence. But the first curfew in the history of Karachi after Independence was clamped on Sept 4, 1947, to help contain communal violence.

A report in the Sept 4 issued said that “Mr N.A. Faruqi, District Magistrate, Karachi, today enforced curfew on the major part of Karachi from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. The curfew will last for three days. It has been imposed under Section 144 CrPC.”

The next day, in the Sept 5 issue, the headline of the lede story on p1 declared, with some relief, that ‘Karachi’s first curfew night passes off peacefully’. The story went on to say that “No incident was reported in the city till Friday afternoon. Shops and other business quarters worked normally and except for the exodus of a large number of Sikhs and [Hindu] Marwaris by sea to ports in Bombay, there was nothing abnormal … in the city.”

The exodus, we were told, “was not because they were afraid of the Muslims in Pakistan, but of the “insanity” of their brethren in the Indian Union.”

Palestine partition

Overseas, the UN’s partition plan for Mandatory Palestine was igniting emotions across the Arab world. As the banner headline on p1 in the Sept 2 issue declared: ‘Arabs to resist Palestine plan by force of arms’. As Israel has expanded its illegal occupation of Palestine over the decades, the Arabs are still resisting.

A news report filed from London declared that “Arab leaders in Jerusalem, Cairo, London and New York last night rejected the recommendations of the United Nations Special Committee for the partition of Palestine as “blatantly unfair” and declared that the Arabs would resist the plan even by the force of arms.”

Meanwhile, armed Zionist gangs such as Irgun called for a “prolonged war against the British” who administered Palestine at the time.

With the advantage of hindsight, one has the opportunity to study the historical cycles in a nation’s life. Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it.

Through this platform, we will look back at the ‘big’ stories that made it to the front pages of Dawn, as well as significant developments tucked away in the inside pages, from the birth of Pakistan onwards, and try to put them in perspective. We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper.

article_html:
The issues of Dawn from Sept 1-7, 1947 chronicled the adoption of the Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order as the country’s working constitution, while the nation’s first commander-in-chief issued a stern call for order to control communal violence. Moreover, the city of Karachi — which has been no stranger to violence over the decades — saw its first curfew as the capital of Pakistan.

Constitutional underpinnings

Constitutional tinkering by powerful, often unelected forces has been a sad constant throughout Pakistan’s history. But as the pages of Dawn in the weeks after independence showed, the country’s founders wanted the country to be run as per the rule of law, not anyone’s personal whims.

The lede story in the Sept 3, 1947, edition noted that “the Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order, an adaptation of the Government of India Act, 1935” would serve as the dominion’s temporary constitution. Of course Pakistan would not have its first proper constitution until 1956, largely owing to the political tumult of the early years.

The Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order sought to do away with the vestiges of empire, and give a fresh direction to the country. The news story noted that the law “does away with expressions like “in his discretion” and “exercising his individual judgment”, found in the India Act.”

“Another important feature is absence of any reference to the King anywhere. All appointments including those of the provincial Governors and High Court Judges, will be made by the Governor-General.” Moreover, the oath of office would be sworn to the “Pakistan Constitution and not to the Crown.”

From these reports, it is clear that the original plan envisaged a farewell to British kings and queens, and constitutional supremacy. Little did the founders of Pakistan know that in the decades to come, many uncrowned local ‘kings’ would trample the Constitution, and attempt to dictate terms to the hapless populace of this country.

The general’s call

Two weeks after independence, the fires of communal violence continued to burn, despite repeated appeals by none other than the Quaid for calm. The situation was such that the Pakistan’s army’s first commander-in-chief — Gen Sir Frank Masservy, a British officer — issued a plea for peace in the Sept 1 issue.

In a special order to all ranks of the army, the C-in-C noted that “our main duty … in conjunction with the civil authorities and the police is the difficult and unpleasant one of maintaining law and order and of stopping bloodshed and murder, looting and arson. …”

The general told his men that there would be zero tolerance for law breakers and other undesirables that were stirring up trouble. “The first type of goondas are goondas, dakus and badmashes. These are enemies of the State and must be hunted out and captured or shot. …

“The second type are ignorant citizens and countrymen who get carried away by feelings of revenge … and vent their wrath on the opposite community with the utmost savagery. These two are also enemies of the State tough they may not realise it. …”

These were certainly stern words from the general. But perhaps desperate times called for desperate measures.

Petrol rationing

Pakistanis, as well as consumers around the world, are paying high prices for gasoline and other fuel products derived from hydrocarbons due to the situation created by the US/Israeli war on Iran. There is also the fear of shortages should things get ugly again in the Gulf; in other countries, there have been riots related to fuel shortages, though Pakistan has thankfully been spared such violence till now.

In Sept 1947, however, the state had to resort to rationing of gasoline as communal disturbances in India had disrupted supplies of coal, putting extra pressure on the available fuel stocks. As a news report highlighted in the Sept 2 issue, “the Government of Pakistan has decided to reduce the present ratio of motor spirit from two gallons per unit to one gallon per unit, in Western Pakistan. This step is taken in order to conserve all the available fuel supply. …”

The decision was made “owing to the disturbances in East Punjab” which had caused interruption in the regular supply of coal to Pakistan from India.

Karachi under curfew

Younger readers, particularly those born in the mid-1990s and thereafter, would not have any memory of a curfew clamped on Karachi. But older readers will recall with dread the days and nights the metropolis used to be placed under curfew during the 1980s and early 1990s due to the rampant political and ethnic violence of those bad old days.

In effect it was an order from the state to shelter in place; unless you had a curfew pass, the law-enforcement agencies — often including the military — would not let you move about freely to quell spasms of violence. But the first curfew in the history of Karachi after Independence was clamped on Sept 4, 1947, to help contain communal violence.

A report in the Sept 4 issued said that “Mr N.A. Faruqi, District Magistrate, Karachi, today enforced curfew on the major part of Karachi from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. The curfew will last for three days. It has been imposed under Section 144 CrPC.”

The next day, in the Sept 5 issue, the headline of the lede story on p1 declared, with some relief, that ‘Karachi’s first curfew night passes off peacefully’. The story went on to say that “No incident was reported in the city till Friday afternoon. Shops and other business quarters worked normally and except for the exodus of a large number of Sikhs and [Hindu] Marwaris by sea to ports in Bombay, there was nothing abnormal … in the city.”

The exodus, we were told, “was not because they were afraid of the Muslims in Pakistan, but of the “insanity” of their brethren in the Indian Union.”

Palestine partition

Overseas, the UN’s partition plan for Mandatory Palestine was igniting emotions across the Arab world. As the banner headline on p1 in the Sept 2 issue declared: ‘Arabs to resist Palestine plan by force of arms’. As Israel has expanded its illegal occupation of Palestine over the decades, the Arabs are still resisting.

A news report filed from London declared that “Arab leaders in Jerusalem, Cairo, London and New York last night rejected the recommendations of the United Nations Special Committee for the partition of Palestine as “blatantly unfair” and declared that the Arabs would resist the plan even by the force of arms.”

Meanwhile, armed Zionist gangs such as Irgun called for a “prolonged war against the British” who administered Palestine at the time.

With the advantage of hindsight, one has the opportunity to study the historical cycles in a nation’s life. Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it.

We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper.

Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it.

Through this platform, we will look back at the ‘big’ stories that made it to the front pages of Dawn, as well as significant developments tucked away in the inside pages, from the birth of Pakistan onwards, and try to put them in perspective. We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper.

headline: Pillion riding, display of weapons banned in KP's Bannu for a week as polio vaccination drive set to begin
description: Restriction also placed on the use of tinted glasses in vehicles.
author: Muhammad Waseem Khan
article_text:
BANNU: The district administration banned pillion riding, display of weapons and use of tinted glasses in vehicles for a week in Bannu on Sunday, keeping in view the commencement of a polio vaccination drive and security concerns.

The ban has been imposed under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The order for the restriction was issued by Deputy Commissioner Bannu Zia ur Rehman Khattak on Saturday, with the ban coming into effect on Sunday. It will remain in force till Nov 7.

The order, seen by Dawn, stated that Bannu’s district police officer (DPO) had informed the administration through an official letter that an anti-polio campaign would be conducted in the district from November 2 to 5.

In view of previous terrorist attacks targeting polio teams and police personnel deployed for their security, as well as the prevailing security situation, precautionary measures were deemed necessary in Bannu, the DC’s order stated.

Under the restriction, the display and exhibition of weapons, pillion riding on motorcycles and the use of tinted glasses in vehicles have been prohibited throughout the district.

However, patwaris (land record keepers) and union council secretaries performing official polio campaign duties have been exempted from the restriction on display of weapons.

The order warned that violators would face legal action under Section 188 (disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant) of the Pakistan Penal Code.

Polio vaccination drive launched

DC Khattak and DPO Shafiullah Gandapur inaugurated the anti-polio campaign in Bannu on Sunday, administering polio drops to children.

The health authorities have set a target of vaccinating 228,000 children under the age of five across 57 union councils of the district, according to a statement issued by the district administration.

Pakistan has reported seven polio cases this year so far, four of which are from Bannu Division.

Bannu Division continues to pose impediments to the government’s efforts to eradicate the virus in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, say officials.

A recent report by the World Health Organisation said it continued to present significant operational and security challenges that impeded implementation of high-quality vaccination activities.

headline: Thousands protest in India's capital against voter roll revision
description: Protesters led by opposition Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi chant “vote thief, leave your seat”.
author: AFP
article_text:
Thousands joined a protest led by opposition politicians in India’s capital on Sunday, renewing demands for the country’s election chief to resign over an overhaul of voter lists they say unfairly benefits the ruling party.

The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests in the world’s largest democracy over the last month.

The Election Commission says the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter lists, but the opposition claims it is being manipulated to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Both the Election Commission and the BJP deny the accusations.

On Sunday, protesters led by opposition Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi chanted “vote thief, leave your seat” and beat drums while marching from central parts of New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan, a large outdoor venue.

“I have been a voter since I was 18 and now I find myself struck off the list,” protester Nandita, 46, told AFP, giving only one name.

“It’s important to be here because of the way things are going. The cost of living is going up… The only option is to take to the streets peacefully.”

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online youth-led protest movement, has also thrown its weight behind the campaign against the voter-roll revision.

The overhaul of India’s voter rolls has resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.

Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.

Members of Hindu-nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

Election authorities say the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries, and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the roll.

Human Rights Watch has said the removal of voters was “arbitrary and deeply flawed”.

“The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalised people their right to vote and other government services,” it said in a statement this week.

The Cockroach movement has been heavily involved in the pushback to the voter-roll revision and several of its leaders were temporarily detained by police during protests last month.

The CJP has gained millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May.

Earlier protests organised by the CJP in July over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration.

The overhaul of India’s voter rolls has resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.
Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Members of Hindu-nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.
Election authorities say the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries, and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the roll.
Human Rights Watch has said the removal of voters was “arbitrary and deeply flawed”.

“The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalised people their right to vote and other government services,” it said in a statement this week.
The Cockroach movement has been heavily involved in the pushback to the voter-roll revision and several of its leaders were temporarily detained by police during protests last month.
The CJP has gained millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May.
Earlier protests organised by the CJP in July over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration.

headline: Till I am here, people of KP will have the first right to its resources: Kundi
description: “No one should think that foreigners will come and loot this province," he says.
author: News Desk
article_text:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi asserted that the people of the province had the first right to its resources.

“No one should think that foreigners will come and loot this province. Till I am here, the people of the province will have the first right to its resources,” he said while addressing a ceremony in Peshawar.

Kundi added that a third party from outside KP, whether a foreigner or from Pakistan, may enter into a joint venture with the people of the province if willing.

The governor, who has assumed the administrative control of KP following the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in the province, assured that his priority was the protection of the people of KP, then of the province itself and then Pakistan.

His assertions follow allegations by Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman that the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in KP was linked to the government’s motive to take control of its resources.

He had also questioned the government’s position on mineral resources during a National Assembly session earlier this week, when he had criticised the Centre over emergency and governor’s rule in KP.

Meanwhile, claims have been circulating on social media that KP’s minerals would be given or sold to the US. This followed a statement made by Chargé d’Affaires Natalie Baker during an interview with The Centrum Media on Sept 30, expressing US interest in Pakistan’s mineral resources.

Kundi, without making any specific mention, said in his address that several reports may be circulating in the media and on social media, but his priority remained the protection of the people of KP.

He said this after outlining the diversity of KP’s resources: “Compared to other provinces, KP has the most natural resources and, as they say: Jahan wasail hotay hen wahan par masail bhi hotay hen (wherever there are resources, there will always be issues). KP is the largest oil and second-largest gas producer in Pakistan, and [..] we produce electricity. We have tourism, mineral resources, and tobacco.”

Kundi also spoke of the Rs160 billion pledged by the federal government for development projects in KP. He said 70 per cent of the funds will be allocated to the 12 districts under the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) and 30pc to other districts.

Kundi assured, “My brothers and sisters in the merged districts will not be deprived of their rightful share.”

On alleged corruption charges against non-functional KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, the governor said if the charges were proven, due legal process would be adopted.

On Friday, adviser to the KP governor on information and public relations Samar Haroon Bilour said that available evidence regarding financial corruption by Afridi was being compiled.

Afridi remains in preventative custody and has not been seen since the imposition of governor’s rule in the province.

The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on October 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. Less than a week after emergency and governor’s rule were imposed in the province, a joint sitting of parliament approved the federal government’s move amid a strong protest from the opposition.

The events of Oct 11 followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI — as well as negotiations to bridge their differences — after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups and asserted that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there.

headline: UAE says hoping for breakthrough yet 'braced for the worst' in Iran-US war
description: The UAE is hoping for a breakthrough in negotiations between Iran and the US while being prepared for the worst, a...
article_text:
The UAE is hoping for a breakthrough in negotiations between Iran and the US while being prepared for the worst, a senior official said, following threats of a resumption of the Middle East war, according to AFP.

“We’re hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough,” diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president Anwar Gargash said during a conference in Manama.

“It is not the interest of the region to go through another round… But I think we’re also, as we’ve shown before, braced for the worst.”

headline: Cyber safety
description: The state of freedom of expression in Pakistan is already quite poor, so any further attempts to clamp down on free speech must be resisted.
author: Editorial
article_text:
WHILE the state’s proposal to create a Cybersecurity and Social Media Awareness Council envisages needed interventions to protect children from online harm, the same body’s focus on ‘fake news’ — as described by the government — is cause for concern.

Speaking at a recent seminar in Islamabad, the federal information minister said there is a need to raise awareness about the “dangers of fake news”, while also emphasising the need for digital education in schools and colleges. In particular, he said children should be protected from cyberattacks. At the same event, the IT minister observed that it was important for both parents and children to know who the latter were interacting with online.

There can be little argument with the fact that cyberspace can be a dangerous place for children. According to a Unicef report, one in 16 children in Pakistan aged 12-17 experienced “at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse” in a single year. This comes to around 1.5m children.

Moreover, the National Commission on the Rights of the Child points out that youngsters are vulnerable to “cyberbullying, online grooming, sharing of sexual abuse materials” and other types of harm. There have been disturbing recent reports of even parents and guardians involved in the online abuse of children. It is, therefore, essential to protect youngsters from online predators through digital literacy, while bringing those involved in these abominable crimes to justice. Pakistan’s children face enough challenges; the state must do all it can to protect them from online harm.

But combining steps against cyberbullying and online abuse of children with the state’s campaign against ‘fake news’ needs to be reconsidered. The state of freedom of expression in Pakistan is already quite poor, so any further attempts to clamp down on free speech must be resisted. Instead, the proposed council should focus on protecting children from dangers in the cyber realm, as well as keeping citizens overall safe from online threats.

headline: Pakistan becomes chair of G-24 bloc of developing nations, reaffirms pledge to fairer global financial system
description: Future of developing economies not peripheral but central to the future of the global economy, says finance minister; PM hopes chairmanship will help Pakistan advocate for global financial reforms.
author: News Desk
article_text:
Pakistan assumed the chairmanship of the Group of 24 (G-24) on Sunday, with Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb expressing the country’s resolve to strengthen the collective voice of developing economies and “advancing a more responsive, fair and development-oriented international financial system”.

The intergovernmental group is a coalition of developing countries established in 1971 to coordinate their positions on international monetary and financial issues, according to its website.

Aurangzeb described its chairmanship as a “profound responsibility”, a handout issued by the Ministry of Finance stated, adding that he also called for “renewed international cooperation, stronger multilateral institutions and reinforced global commitments to address climate shocks, development financing gaps and global economic fragmentation”.

“The future of developing economies is not peripheral to the future of the global economy. It is central to it,” the statement quoted the finance minister as saying.

He further highlighted the “immense potential of emerging and developing nations as drivers of investment, innovation, entrepreneurship and global growth”.

Aurangzeb outlined three strategic priorities for Pakistan under the G-24 chairmanship: placing development at the centre of global economic policymaking, strengthening multilateral frameworks, and advancing a development-oriented international financial architecture.

For the first priority, the finance minister stressed the importance of macroeconomic stability, saying it must underpin investment, productivity, employment, and shared prosperity.

He added that such an approach would enable “developing and low-income economies to move beyond crisis management towards sustainable growth”.

Secondly, he added that under its chairmanship, Pakistan would advocate for “more equitable and fair governance, meaningful participation in decision-making and greater responsiveness of the Bretton Woods institutions to the evolving needs and realities of their members”.

Thirdly, the finance minister said Pakistan would prioritise affordable and timely development financing, sustainable debt solutions, stronger global financial safety nets, climate resilience and greater mobilisation of public and private capital.

“Our task is to ensure that the immense potential of developing economies is not constrained by an international financial architecture that has yet to fully adapt to a changing world,” Aurangzeb was quoted as saying.

The finance minister emphasised aligning financial stability with long-term development objectives, drawing on Pakistan’s experience with economic stabilisation, reform and resilience, the statement said.

He added that this would ensure that reforming economies have the necessary financing and policy space to pursue sustainable growth.

Aurangzeb further stated that Pakistan’s tenure as the chair would be guided by “G-24’s longstanding principles of consultation, consensus and collective advocacy, working closely with members across Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, alongside the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and other international partners, to translate shared priorities into practical outcomes.”

The finance czar acknowledged outgoing chair Nigeria’s leadership and pledged to build on the group’s progress.

He further emphasised that the “effectiveness of collective leadership must be judged by tangible development outcomes”.

“The true measure of our collective leadership will not simply be the strength of our voice, but the difference that voice makes,” the ministry quoted him as saying.

According to the statement, Aurangzeb reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to advancing G-24’s mission “from collective voice to collective influence, and from collective influence to meaningful progress”.

‘Significant diplomatic milestone’

President Asif Ali Zardari hailed Pakistan’s assumption of the G24 chairmanship and congratulated Aurangzeb along with the relevant team.

In a statement on X, he said the development was an “important” opportunity for the “effective” representation of developing countries in global economic affairs.

“This opportunity will provide Pakistan with the chance to play a role in developmental financing, climate challenges, and promoting global financial cooperation,” the president asserted.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also welcomed the development, calling it a “significant diplomatic milestone” and expressing hope that the chairmanship would provide Pakistan “an opportunity to play an influential role in advocating for necessary reforms within the global financial system, securing equitable financial support to address climate change and promoting sustainable development opportunities for emerging economies”, a statement issued by his office said.

He also lauded the finance minister and his team for their “tireless efforts, effective diplomacy, and professional competence”.

The premier further commended the team for ensuring “impactful” participation at the recently held annual meetings of the World Bank and the IMF, which he said helped Pakistan secure a “prominent position in the economic leadership of developing nations”.

headline: Cyber safety
description: The state of freedom of expression in Pakistan is already quite poor, so any further attempts to clamp down on free speech must be resisted.
author: Editorial
article_text:
WHILE the state’s proposal to create a Cybersecurity and Social Media Awareness Council envisages needed interventions to protect children from online harm, the same body’s focus on ‘fake news’ — as described by the government — is cause for concern.

Speaking at a recent seminar in Islamabad, the federal information minister said there is a need to raise awareness about the “dangers of fake news”, while also emphasising the need for digital education in schools and colleges. In particular, he said children should be protected from cyberattacks. At the same event, the IT minister observed that it was important for both parents and children to know who the latter were interacting with online.

There can be little argument with the fact that cyberspace can be a dangerous place for children. According to a Unicef report, one in 16 children in Pakistan aged 12-17 experienced “at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse” in a single year. This comes to around 1.5m children.

Moreover, the National Commission on the Rights of the Child points out that youngsters are vulnerable to “cyberbullying, online grooming, sharing of sexual abuse materials” and other types of harm. There have been disturbing recent reports of even parents and guardians involved in the online abuse of children. It is, therefore, essential to protect youngsters from online predators through digital literacy, while bringing those involved in these abominable crimes to justice. Pakistan’s children face enough challenges; the state must do all it can to protect them from online harm.

But combining steps against cyberbullying and online abuse of children with the state’s campaign against ‘fake news’ needs to be reconsidered. The state of freedom of expression in Pakistan is already quite poor, so any further attempts to clamp down on free speech must be resisted. Instead, the proposed council should focus on protecting children from dangers in the cyber realm, as well as keeping citizens overall safe from online threats.

Published in Dawn, November 1st, 2026

headline: PIA's first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner arrives in Islamabad
description: PIA becomes the first Pakistani airline to have added a Boeing 787-9 to its fleet.
author: News Desk
article_text:
Pakistan International Airlines’ (PIA) first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, acquired on lease last month, arrived in Islamabad from London as flight PK786 on Sunday.

A PIA spokesperson, in a statement, said that the carrier is the first Pakistani airline to have added a Boeing 787-9 to its fleet.

PIA Chief Executive Aamir Hayat, accompanied by his team, welcomed the Dreamliner at Islamabad airport, according to the statement.

The plane is equipped with modern technology, including in-flight entertainment, and features a spacious and comfortable cabin, PIA said.

“The inclusion of the Dreamliner is part of a strategy to modernise PIA’s fleet and strengthen its international network,” the spokesperson said.

“PIA’s objective is to provide international-standard travel facilities and a more comfortable air travel experience to passengers through modern aircraft.”

The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is a long-range, twin-engine plane with up to 325 seats. Previously, PIA’s fleet consisted of 12 Boeing 777 jets, 15 Airbus A320 planes and five smaller ATRs.

Last month, PIA signed an ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance) lease agreement with Norse Atlantic Airways to acquire two state-of-the-art Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners, one of which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday.

A PIA spokesperson at the time said the addition of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner would mark the start of the airline’s expansion.

By expanding its fleet, the airline aims to meet rising demand with direct flights and broader global connectivity, he added.

The aircraft would operate direct long-haul flights from Pakistan to the United Kingdom, he said, adding that they would support PIA operations between different points in the UK and Pakistan.

The development also comes as the government in September clarified that it was not buying any aircraft for the former national carrier after reports emerged of a federal minister arranging and negotiating sovereign-linked financing for PIA jets.

PIA was privatised in December last year through an auction. A consortium led by Arif Habib Corporation Limited had won the auction for 75 per cent shares of PIA in December last year, making a winning bid of Rs135 billion. The Arif Habib-led consortium had vowed to transform the loss-making airline through operational restructuring, fleet expansion, and improved customer service.

headline: Iran submits evidence of US-Israeli attacks on maritime infrastructure to IMO, warns of safety risks: state media
description: Iran has submitted documents and photographic evidence of US and Israeli attacks on the country’s ports, civilian...
article_text:
Iran has submitted documents and photographic evidence of US and Israeli attacks on the country’s ports, civilian vessels, and maritime infrastructure to the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), warning that the damage poses serious risks to maritime safety across the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Sea of Oman, state-run IRNA reports.

The report warns that damage to maritime traffic control systems could increase the risk of vessel collisions and secondary accidents, while the destruction of rescue facilities could undermine emergency response capabilities and endanger the lives of foreign seafarers.

The report warns that damage to maritime traffic control systems could increase the risk of vessel collisions and secondary accidents, while the destruction of rescue facilities could undermine emergency response capabilities and endanger the lives of foreign seafarers.

headline: Upper Dir police claim arresting 5 suspects over alleged assault of minor boy
description: Teenage boy complained to police after incident of video was circulated on social media.
author: Haleem Asad
article_text:
LOWER DIR: Police in Upper Dir said on Sunday they have arrested five of the six suspects over the alleged assault and intimidation of a teenage boy, a purported video of which was circulated on social media.

Wari Circle Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) Fakhr-i-Alam confirmed the arrests to Dawn.

The incident took place on Oct 25, according to a first information report (FIR), dated Oct 30 and seen by Dawn, filed by Wari police on the boy’s complaint.

The case invoked Sections 364-A (kidnapping or abducting an underage person), 342 (punishment for wrongful confinement), 506 (criminal intimidation), 147 (rioting) and 149 (unlawful assembly) of the Pakistan Penal Code.

In the FIR, the boy alleged that on the day of the incident, a friend of his called him to a place where two men, including an unidentified tehsildar, forcibly made him board a car and took him to an under-construction house in Shinkarai.

There, he was allegedly assaulted and threatened by the two men who demanded an “unnatural” act.

The FIR nominated a total of six people, including his friend. Those arrested excluded one of the two men who made the boy board the car.

The boy alleged that the two men who forced him into the car and three others present at the house kept him confined in a room for around three hours.

The complainant further alleged that the two men who brought him there and another person recorded the incident on their mobile phones, while two others delivered blows to him with kicks, punches, and sticks.

“Due to their blows, I sustained severe pain in my right shin, right and left arms, and across the rest of my body,” the boy said in the FIR.

The complainant further claimed that the incident stemmed from WhatsApp conversations among friends.

According to the complainant, the delay in reporting the incident was due to death threats from the suspects, who had also threatened to share the video. The video, reportedly recorded by some of the suspects, surfaced on social media days after the alleged incident, prompting police to take action.

The allegations levelled in the FIR have yet to be independently verified by Dawn. Police said they had initiated an investigation into the case.

Child protection NGO Sahil estimates that at least 558 cases of child abductions were reported across the country in the first six months of 2026.

Earlier this month, police in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Charsadda arrested a man for allegedly assaulting a five-year-old boy. In late August, Mansehra police held two men after a mother alleged they assaulted her nine-year-old son.

headline: Iran can’t be allowed ‘to take global economy hostage’: US official
description: State Department official Donald Blome says the United States has extended a hand in negotiations to Iran, but it’s...
article_text:
State Department official Donald Blome says the United States has extended a hand in negotiations to Iran, but it’s prepared to go the opposite way if the Strait of Hormuz doesn’t return to normal, Al Jazeera reports.

Blome, US assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern Affairs, spoke at the Manama Dialogue, a security forum held in Bahrain.

“The hand of negotiation has been extended, and those channels have continued to be open and active,” Blome said.

“At the same time, we’ve been also prepared to go in another direction. We just can’t allow Iran to take this region and the global economy hostage.”

headline: Consultations ongoing over Hormuz plan but conclusion depends on US answer to Iran's offer: Araghchi
description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says consultations with Qatari mediators over reopening the Strait of Hormuz...
article_text:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says consultations with Qatari mediators over reopening the Strait of Hormuz continue but the United States will need to respond to its offer, Al Jazeera reports citing state media.

“Consultations are ongoing but we have not yet reached a definitive conclusion because this conclusion depends on the answers the other side gives to our questions,” Araghchi said. “There was no plan to negotiate with the American side during this trip.”

He made the comments on the sidelines of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee meeting, according to state-run IRNA news agency.

Araghchi emphasised that Tehran remains firm on its seven previously stated conditions and is awaiting a US response. Iranian authorities have signalled that a deal remains possible, provided their demands are implemented.

headline: US hears Pakistan’s concerns over terrorism from Afghanistan, would play ‘productive role’ if there is one: Rubio
description: "We're against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets," US secretary of state says.
author: News Desk
article_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said that Washington has “heard” Pakistan’s concerns about terrorism emanating from Afghanistan and if “there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it”.

Rubio’s statement came in response to a question about tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan at a press talks in Atlanta.

“Pakistan is concerned about terrorist attacks that are being sponsored from the territory of Afghanistan. They feel as if the Taliban have not done enough to constrain those attacks, and they have taken action against it.

“We obviously have heard those concerns on their part. We obviously don’t want them to be targeted for terrorism. So if there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it,” Rubio said.

Mentioning that the US did not “necessarily [have] the closest relationship” with the Afghan Taliban, Rubio added: “We’ve heard the concerns that Pakistan has raised and we’ve seen some of those attacks that they point to. We’re against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets.”

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), that it says are used for attacks in Pakistan.

For their part, the Afghan Taliban have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad’s allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan.

On Saturday, Pakistan’s information ministry rebuked the Afghan Taliban’s stance on the ongoing conflict between the two countries, assailing its “persistent refusal to address terrorism” emanating from Afghanistan’s soil.

The statement came in response to remarks made by Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, who blamed Islamabad’s “wrong policies” for preventing a resolution to the conflict and insisted Kabul was not the cause of counterterrorism issues.

In its response, the information ministry said the Afghan spokesman’s remarks expose the “regime’s deeply misguided approach and unwillingness to confront the root cause of deteriorating relations with Pakistan”.

“The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” it added.

Islamabad reiterated that the “Taliban regime’s persistent refusal to address terrorism remains the principal obstacle to normal relations”.

Multiple rounds of talks between the two sides last year, facilitated by Qatar and Turkiye, failed to bring about any workable solution, with the Pakistani government saying the Taliban officials gave no assurances on the key issues. Efforts this year made with China’s involvement also resulted in no breakthrough.

Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has also recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement.

Moscow’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had last month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan.

When asked about it during a weekly media briefing, Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan had said talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional. He also rejected suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour, saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute.

He further stated: “At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion.”

Meanwhile, intermittent skirmishes at the border continue.

September witnessed yet another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Those skirmishes continued in October with Pakistani security forces responding to unprovoked fire from the Afghan side along the border in Kurram and Lower South Waziristan’s Angoor Adda, according to security sources.

article_html:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said that Washington has “heard” Pakistan’s concerns about terrorism emanating from Afghanistan and if “there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it”.

Rubio’s statement came in response to a question about tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan at a press talks in Atlanta.

“Pakistan is concerned about terrorist attacks that are being sponsored from the territory of Afghanistan. They feel as if the Taliban have not done enough to constrain those attacks, and they have taken action against it.

“We obviously have heard those concerns on their part. We obviously don’t want them to be targeted for terrorism. So if there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it,” Rubio said.

Mentioning that the US did not “necessarily [have] the closest relationship” with the Afghan Taliban, Rubio added: “We’ve heard the concerns that Pakistan has raised and we’ve seen some of those attacks that they point to. We’re against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets.”

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), that it says are used for attacks in Pakistan.

For their part, the Afghan Taliban have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad’s allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan.

On Saturday, Pakistan’s information ministry rebuked the Afghan Taliban’s stance on the ongoing conflict between the two countries, assailing its “persistent refusal to address terrorism” emanating from Afghanistan’s soil.

The statement came in response to remarks made by Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, who blamed Islamabad’s “wrong policies” for preventing a resolution to the conflict and insisted Kabul was not the cause of counterterrorism issues.

In its response, the information ministry said the Afghan spokesman’s remarks expose the “regime’s deeply misguided approach and unwillingness to confront the root cause of deteriorating relations with Pakistan”.

“The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” it added.

Islamabad reiterated that the “Taliban regime’s persistent refusal to address terrorism remains the principal obstacle to normal relations”.

Multiple rounds of talks between the two sides last year, facilitated by Qatar and Turkiye, failed to bring about any workable solution, with the Pakistani government saying the Taliban officials gave no assurances on the key issues. Efforts this year made with China’s involvement also resulted in no breakthrough.

Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has also recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement.

Moscow’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had last month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan.

When asked about it during a weekly media briefing, Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan had said talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional. He also rejected suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour, saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute.

He further stated: “At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion.”

Meanwhile, intermittent skirmishes at the border continue.

September witnessed yet another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Those skirmishes continued in October with Pakistani security forces responding to unprovoked fire from the Afghan side along the border in Kurram and Lower South Waziristan’s Angoor Adda, according to security sources.

headline: Pakistan’s past and future make a bid for the present
description: As Pakistan build up to the World Cup next year, Saturday’s standout performances by three different southpaws showed how the past and future can culminate for present glory.
author: Rameen Salman
article_text:
Whatever there is to be said about Fakhar Zaman has been said.

And he has usually said it himself – first when he made his debut and steered Pakistan to their greatest triumph of the past decade, then countless times for Lahore Qalandars, then on that one rainy day in Bangalore, climbing a mountain no one had given him a shot at.

Fakhar has had a long few years, with recurring injuries and patches of very lean form, but his penchant of showing up when it matters, in extremely emphatic fashion, hasn’t wavered with time.

In a side that gets frequently noted for crumbling under pressure, faltering in the biggest moments, never being quite able to get over the line for true glory, Fakhar has churned out a reputation for himself that is the opposite.

A ‘big match player’ is the sort of cliche that seems overwrought, but Fakhar has made it entirely his own. When it matters most, it is foolish to count him out.

“The way my last 4 games had gone, a good performance was due,” he said during the post-match ceremony after scoring a match-winning century to lead Pakistan to triumph in the One-day International tri-series final against Sri Lanka on Saturday.

“Cricket is just like this, sometimes you are a good knick and sometimes you don’t score; even today I was struggling in the beginning.”

“But I know that when it is my day, and the ball is coming onto my bat, I will score big.”

And that he did – despite his lean returns in the first four matches Pakistan played in this tri-series, and despite the several scares he survived yesterday - wobbly shots, being dropped and given reprieves, Fakhar showed why giving him a life in a final has been, historically, a bad idea.

Pakistan does not have a lot of time left with Fakhar. He is 36 years old, and will be 37 by the time next year’s World Cup in southern Africa is underway.

It would probably be the most opportune moment for him to sign off on a memorable career, trying to give his team one shot at the ultimate glory in his favourite format.

His century yesterday - 12th in ODIs, a record-breaking fourth in chases of more than 300 - is just one of those things Pakistan fans should learn to cherish when they get.

But if yesterday showed anything, apart from reaffirming what Fakhar means to a Pakistan side, it was that Pakistan don’t have to be starved of time.

In a match where Pakistan’s most trustworthy southpaw wielded his bat once again, it was one other that let him, and yet another that ensured it wouldn’t go to waste.

Saad Baig had big shoes to fill coming into this ODI tri-nation series. With Mohammad Rizwan’s absence, Pakistan was not only missing a cog of the batting line-up that has been so crucial for so long, but also one of the finest pair of wicket-keeping gloves the country has sported.

No one else has seemed good enough in comparison behind the stumps - either too undercooked, or too sloppy.

Saad was Pakistan’s U-19 captain, and made his debut earlier in this tri-series. With a promising performance behind the stumps, and a string of starts with the bat that left one feeling unfulfilled but entirely assured of the pristine talent that shone through, the 19-year-old came out looking like he had a lot to prove.

Ironically, he turns 20 today, following a knock yesterday that can only be described as a coming-of-age.

If Fakhar was Pakistan’s anti-thesis to not showing up when it matters, Saad was the anti-thesis to a star performing batter never having enough support on the other end.

“I have played domestic cricket with Saad, he is a very talented player,” Fakhar said, adding that Saad briskly scoring runs when he came to the crease yesterday allowed Fakhar to settle and take his time, and ultimately go big.

“The credit goes to him for starting the way he did.”

“Obviously there is pressure on you whenever you move to international cricket,” said Saad in a video reflection posted on PCB’s social media handles.

“But the way you have to play through the pressure and back yourself, I was lacking that in the first two or three games, and was getting out in the 30s,” he added, saying that his plan for yesterday’s innings was to score while staying settled at the crease, and Fakhar’s “outstanding” innings made doing that all the more easier.

He rotated strike and got into a good groove with Fakhar, rotating strike and picking out the Sri Lankan bowlers whenever the opportunity came to him. Perhaps the way he got out - an anticlimactic chip back to the bowler on a full Theekshana delivery - reflects where he stands in his career compared to the man across the other end, lacking just the final bit of grit and presence that can only come with time.

And if these two left-handers set Pakistan on for victory, another one entirely made sure he finished it.

Between overs 32.5 and 42.5, Pakistan did not score a single boundary. Fakhar and Salman Ali Agha had been bowled in quick succession.

With Hasan Nawaz and Arafat new on the crease, and most of the toe-end of the innings left to bat through, their game plan seemed simple enough: don’t throw it away.

The scoring during those overs came entirely from rotating strike, which might have felt grinding and underwhelming for an audience who had just witnessed a Fakhar Zaman special.

It was a full Asitha Fernando delivery in the 45th over, drilled disdainfully down the ground, that would open the floodgates.

In the bowler’s next over, Arafat hit possibly the cleanest, most sublime sequence of shots he has procured in his short career so far, bludgeoning two sixes and a four before holing out with Pakistan just two short of the win.

“When I went in [to bat], I told Hasan that we have been through this situation before, and so we tried building a partnership,” he said. The two had carried out a deftly executed rescue job in their first tri-series fixture against England as well, ensuring Pakistan posted a total north of 300.

“We backed each other and waited for bad balls to come to us.”

“And I think through communicating with each other we had developed confidence in one another as well,” he said.

Arafat was awarded player of the series as well - the second time he’s been awarded the title in as many ODI series he has participated in.

“I have been saying from the beginning that I am an all-rounder,” he said in the ceremony. He was, after all, the leading architect with both bat and ball in Pakistan’s first win against England.

“There is pressure, but the way you enjoy the pressure, stay calm during it, and execute your skills is important,” he said of the tricky place the team found itself in when he came in to bat with Hasan.

Pakistan’s ODI assignments now all build up to the big shot at the big prize, the World Cup in South Africa next year. Young talents like Saad and Arafat is blooding in, and stalwarts like Fakhar hoping to find one final burst for the nation.

What Pakistan can hope to take to South Africa is a team that sports both, the best of its recent past, and the most promising of its hopefully long future. And three left-handers on Saturday night in Lahore, showed exactly how to do it.

article_html:
Whatever there is to be said about Fakhar Zaman has been said.

And he has usually said it himself – first when he made his debut and steered Pakistan to their greatest triumph of the past decade, then countless times for Lahore Qalandars, then on that one rainy day in Bangalore, climbing a mountain no one had given him a shot at.

Fakhar has had a long few years, with recurring injuries and patches of very lean form, but his penchant of showing up when it matters, in extremely emphatic fashion, hasn’t wavered with time.

In a side that gets frequently noted for crumbling under pressure, faltering in the biggest moments, never being quite able to get over the line for true glory, Fakhar has churned out a reputation for himself that is the opposite.

A ‘big match player’ is the sort of cliche that seems overwrought, but Fakhar has made it entirely his own. When it matters most, it is foolish to count him out.

“The way my last 4 games had gone, a good performance was due,” he said during the post-match ceremony after scoring a match-winning century to lead Pakistan to triumph in the One-day International tri-series final against Sri Lanka on Saturday.

“Cricket is just like this, sometimes you are a good knick and sometimes you don’t score; even today I was struggling in the beginning.”

“But I know that when it is my day, and the ball is coming onto my bat, I will score big.”

And that he did – despite his lean returns in the first four matches Pakistan played in this tri-series, and despite the several scares he survived yesterday - wobbly shots, being dropped and given reprieves, Fakhar showed why giving him a life in a final has been, historically, a bad idea.

Pakistan does not have a lot of time left with Fakhar. He is 36 years old, and will be 37 by the time next year’s World Cup in southern Africa is underway.

It would probably be the most opportune moment for him to sign off on a memorable career, trying to give his team one shot at the ultimate glory in his favourite format.

His century yesterday - 12th in ODIs, a record-breaking fourth in chases of more than 300 - is just one of those things Pakistan fans should learn to cherish when they get.

But if yesterday showed anything, apart from reaffirming what Fakhar means to a Pakistan side, it was that Pakistan don’t have to be starved of time.

In a match where Pakistan’s most trustworthy southpaw wielded his bat once again, it was one other that let him, and yet another that ensured it wouldn’t go to waste.

Saad Baig had big shoes to fill coming into this ODI tri-nation series. With Mohammad Rizwan’s absence, Pakistan was not only missing a cog of the batting line-up that has been so crucial for so long, but also one of the finest pair of wicket-keeping gloves the country has sported.

No one else has seemed good enough in comparison behind the stumps - either too undercooked, or too sloppy.

Saad was Pakistan’s U-19 captain, and made his debut earlier in this tri-series. With a promising performance behind the stumps, and a string of starts with the bat that left one feeling unfulfilled but entirely assured of the pristine talent that shone through, the 19-year-old came out looking like he had a lot to prove.

Ironically, he turns 20 today, following a knock yesterday that can only be described as a coming-of-age.

If Fakhar was Pakistan’s anti-thesis to not showing up when it matters, Saad was the anti-thesis to a star performing batter never having enough support on the other end.

“I have played domestic cricket with Saad, he is a very talented player,” Fakhar said, adding that Saad briskly scoring runs when he came to the crease yesterday allowed Fakhar to settle and take his time, and ultimately go big.

“The credit goes to him for starting the way he did.”

“Obviously there is pressure on you whenever you move to international cricket,” said Saad in a video reflection posted on PCB’s social media handles.

“But the way you have to play through the pressure and back yourself, I was lacking that in the first two or three games, and was getting out in the 30s,” he added, saying that his plan for yesterday’s innings was to score while staying settled at the crease, and Fakhar’s “outstanding” innings made doing that all the more easier.

He rotated strike and got into a good groove with Fakhar, rotating strike and picking out the Sri Lankan bowlers whenever the opportunity came to him. Perhaps the way he got out - an anticlimactic chip back to the bowler on a full Theekshana delivery - reflects where he stands in his career compared to the man across the other end, lacking just the final bit of grit and presence that can only come with time.

And if these two left-handers set Pakistan on for victory, another one entirely made sure he finished it.

Between overs 32.5 and 42.5, Pakistan did not score a single boundary. Fakhar and Salman Ali Agha had been bowled in quick succession.

With Hasan Nawaz and Arafat new on the crease, and most of the toe-end of the innings left to bat through, their game plan seemed simple enough: don’t throw it away.

The scoring during those overs came entirely from rotating strike, which might have felt grinding and underwhelming for an audience who had just witnessed a Fakhar Zaman special.

It was a full Asitha Fernando delivery in the 45th over, drilled disdainfully down the ground, that would open the floodgates.

In the bowler’s next over, Arafat hit possibly the cleanest, most sublime sequence of shots he has procured in his short career so far, bludgeoning two sixes and a four before holing out with Pakistan just two short of the win.

“When I went in [to bat], I told Hasan that we have been through this situation before, and so we tried building a partnership,” he said. The two had carried out a deftly executed rescue job in their first tri-series fixture against England as well, ensuring Pakistan posted a total north of 300.

“We backed each other and waited for bad balls to come to us.”

“And I think through communicating with each other we had developed confidence in one another as well,” he said.

Arafat was awarded player of the series as well - the second time he’s been awarded the title in as many ODI series he has participated in.

“I have been saying from the beginning that I am an all-rounder,” he said in the ceremony. He was, after all, the leading architect with both bat and ball in Pakistan’s first win against England.

“There is pressure, but the way you enjoy the pressure, stay calm during it, and execute your skills is important,” he said of the tricky place the team found itself in when he came in to bat with Hasan.

Pakistan’s ODI assignments now all build up to the big shot at the big prize, the World Cup in South Africa next year. Young talents like Saad and Arafat is blooding in, and stalwarts like Fakhar hoping to find one final burst for the nation.

What Pakistan can hope to take to South Africa is a team that sports both, the best of its recent past, and the most promising of its hopefully long future. And three left-handers on Saturday night in Lahore, showed exactly how to do it.

headline: Sialkot police say 6 held as TikToker nominated in case over stampede at mehndi event
description: Police say efforts under way to apprehend the TikTok influencer; deaths rise to 2; NOC revoked over violations of terms.
author: Abid Mahmood
article_text:
NAROWAL: Sialkot police on Sunday said they had arrested six suspects and registered a case after a stampede at a mehndi (henna) event, the deaths from which have risen to two.

TikToker Muhammad Ansar Jatt, known as “Mr Pattlo”, had announced holding a mehndi event and prize-distribution ceremony at Faraz Cricket Ground on Daska Road on Friday night.

With hundreds gathered at the site, a stampede occurred when the stadium gates opened. While Rescue 1122 initially said one man had died and 13 others were injured, residents had put the number of injured higher because many were taken to nearby hospitals by attendees at the event.

On Sunday, Sialkot Police said 18 people were injured in the stampede. One of them succumbed to his injuries at a government hospital, taking the deaths to two, the public relations officer for the district police officer (DPO) confirmed.

Noting that Jatt had immediately fled the scene after the incident, police said their investigation and raid teams were conducting operations to apprehend the TikTok influencer.

The police statement added that they had taken 50 motorcycles and a car — intended for Friday’s lucky draw — into their custody.

Sialkot DPO Dost Muhammad confirmed the arrest of six individuals involved in managing the event.

He added that police teams have been constituted to apprehend the remaining suspects with the help of modern technology, human intelligence sources, and traditional policing methods.

The retired captain noted that according to preliminary police investigations, organisers had invited a large number of people by advertising a lucky draw featuring prizes such as motorcycles, a car and other valuable items via social media.

During the event, an announcement was made over the loudspeakers instructing all attendees to enter the grounds simultaneously. This simultaneous entry into the sports stadium triggered a severe stampede, the DPO said.

He stated that the organisers violated the terms of their permit, as well as established safety standard operating procedures (SOPs). The stampede also disrupted the flow of traffic on the main Daska-Sialkot Road.

Noting reports of unruly behaviour by attendees and damage to public and private property, DPO Muhammad emphasised that protecting citizens’ lives and property is the police’s primary responsibility.

“Negligence regarding safety arrangements at any public gathering or event which puts human lives at risk cannot be permitted,” he said.

The Sialkot DPO declared that legal action would be taken against all those responsible for the incident, without any discrimination.

NOC revoked

According to a spokesperson for the Sialkot district administration, a no-objection certificate (NOC) had been issued to the TikToker for holding a mehfil-i-samaa (a gathering for devotional music/poetry) during a private event within an enclosed space in Daska.

The spokesperson stated that the event was cancelled before it could even begin, due to violations of the stipulated terms and conditions. According to the spokesperson, the NOC specified that the programme was to commence after the Isha (night) prayers on Friday.

However, reports were received regarding alleged irregularities in the event arrangements by the organisers as early as 4pm.

Upon reviewing the reports, Sialkot Deputy Commissioner Awais Mushtaq took immediate preemptive action and revoked the previously issued NOC.

FIR registered

The first information report (FIR), dated Oct 31 and available with Dawn, was registered at the Motra Police Station on the complaint of Inspector Mubeen Ahmed.

The FIR names Jatt, his brother, the owner of Faraz Cricket Ground, and six others who were organisers of the event, as well as 40-45 unidentified security guards.

It invoked sections 322 (punishment for qatl-bis-sabab), 188 (disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant), 148 (rioting, armed with deadly weapon), 149 (every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object), 431 (mischief by injury to public road, bridge, river or channel), 440 (mischief committed after preparation made for causing death or hurt), and 109 (abetment if the act abetted committed in consequence) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), along with Section 16 of the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) Ordinance.

In the FIR, the inspector accused the suspects of violating the terms of the permit granted by the Sialkot district administration, as well as the established SOPs.

The alleged violations included the misuse of loudspeakers, the blocking of a main road, the vandalism of citizens’ motorcycles, and the infliction of loss of life and property.

The FIR noted that a large crowd managed to enter the Faraz Sports Stadium due to inadequate security arrangements at the venue.

According to the FIR, dozens of attendees at the mehndi and prize distribution ceremony reported that their mobile phones had gone missing and unidentified thieves picked their pockets, depriving them of cash and important documents.

NAROWAL: Sialkot police on Sunday said they had arrested six suspects and registered a case after a stampede at a mehndi (henna) event, the deaths from which have risen to two.

TikToker Muhammad Ansar Jatt, known as “Mr Pattlo”, had announced holding a mehndi event and prize-distribution ceremony at Faraz Cricket Ground on Daska Road on Friday night.

With hundreds gathered at the site, a stampede occurred when the stadium gates opened. While Rescue 1122 initially said one man had died and 13 others were injured, residents had put the number of injured higher because many were taken to nearby hospitals by attendees at the event.

On Sunday, Sialkot Police said 18 people were injured in the stampede. One of them succumbed to his injuries at a government hospital, taking the deaths to two, the public relations officer for the district police officer (DPO) confirmed.

Noting that Jatt had immediately fled the scene after the incident, police said their investigation and raid teams were conducting operations to apprehend the TikTok influencer.

The police statement added that they had taken 50 motorcycles and a car — intended for Friday’s lucky draw — into their custody.

Sialkot DPO Dost Muhammad confirmed the arrest of six individuals involved in managing the event.

He added that police teams have been constituted to apprehend the remaining suspects with the help of modern technology, human intelligence sources, and traditional policing methods.

The retired captain noted that according to preliminary police investigations, organisers had invited a large number of people by advertising a lucky draw featuring prizes such as motorcycles, a car and other valuable items via social media.

During the event, an announcement was made over the loudspeakers instructing all attendees to enter the grounds simultaneously. This simultaneous entry into the sports stadium triggered a severe stampede, the DPO said.

He stated that the organisers violated the terms of their permit, as well as established safety standard operating procedures (SOPs). The stampede also disrupted the flow of traffic on the main Daska-Sialkot Road.

Noting reports of unruly behaviour by attendees and damage to public and private property, DPO Muhammad emphasised that protecting citizens’ lives and property is the police’s primary responsibility.

“Negligence regarding safety arrangements at any public gathering or event which puts human lives at risk cannot be permitted,” he said.

The Sialkot DPO declared that legal action would be taken against all those responsible for the incident, without any discrimination.

The FIR names Jatt, his brother, the owner of Faraz Cricket Ground, and six others who were organisers of the event, as well as 40-45 unidentified security guards.

The alleged violations included the misuse of loudspeakers, the blocking of a main road, the vandalism of citizens’ motorcycles, and the infliction of loss of life and property.

The FIR noted that a large crowd managed to enter the Faraz Sports Stadium due to inadequate security arrangements at the venue.

headline: Iran’s Araghchi says he hopes for ‘rationality’ from US
description: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Tehran was expecting rationality from the US, Al Jazeera reports. “We...
article_text:
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Tehran was expecting rationality from the US, Al Jazeera reports.

“We are making our efforts in this direction and hope that there is rationality on the other side to prefer diplomacy to other paths,” Araghchi said.

Araghchi added that orders issued by Iran’s supreme commander-in-chief to senior military officials had clearly demonstrated Tehran’s resolve.

“Our armed forces also have a very clear mission and, drawing on the experiences of the past two wars, are much stronger than before.”
